SESSION: 2026-04-21 (Session 18, continuing — R62 FRG infrastructure)
VERSIONS: Acervator 3.13.7 (no bump) / SADP 1.17 → 1.18
TITLE: Structural Freshness Enforcement — Ending R26 Drift
================================================================================

The R26 violation documented in the previous entry was caught by the
operator. The fix (back-fill the Chronicle) addressed the immediate
symptom. This entry documents the structural fix that prevents recurrence.

WHAT WAS BUILT:
  • sadp/freshness.py — structural drift detection runner. Eight initial
    checks, each as a pure function:
       R26 — Chronicle ≥ max(CHANGELOG, HOP addendum)
       R26 — root + sadp/ Chronicle copies byte-identical
       R51 — src/__init__.py __version__ == main.py current_version
       R50 — ACTIVE_ANCHORS.md ≥ EPISODIC_MEMORY.json
       HOP — header counts match body + canonical sources
       PM  — docs/tools/build_product_manual.py VERSION == code version
       R49 — EDIT_LOG.jsonl ≥ EPISODIC_MEMORY.json
       R50 — recent MEMs reference only registered rules
    Adding a new invariant is one FreshnessCheck entry. Exit code 1 blocks
    proceeding; 0 is READY.
  • sadp/hop_open.py — deterministic 6-step hop-open command matching the
    operator's exact specification (READ SADP / READ CHRONICLE / READ PM /
    READ ORDERS / FRESHNESS / VERDICT). Three modes: default (handshake),
    --query (ask operator for next task), --proceed (proceed per orders).
  • R62 FRG registered in RULE_REGISTRY.json — Group JJ, depends on R26,
    R28, R49, R50, R51. Formalizes the structural-enforcement discipline.
  • NEXT_SESSION_ORDERS.md ORDER 0 rewritten: the session runs the command
    and responds to its exit code, not to interpretation of a paragraph.

KEY DECISIONS & RATIONALE:
  • Why structural instead of textual. The previous session closed with a
    loud written warning about R26. That warning did not prevent the
    violation it warned against — a later session simply did not read it.
    Rules enforced by text alone decay. Rules enforced by a check that
    runs every cascade are either passing or failing, nothing in between.
    R62 FRG codifies this principle so future rules have a natural home.
  • Why one function per invariant. The operator's phrase was "short-term
    rule memory loops." The model is: each rule that has an omission-
    failure mode gets a function whose sole job is to notice the omission.
    Registry makes enumeration cheap; pure functions make each check
    independently testable; exit code makes integration with any cascade
    script trivial.
  • Why grace periods. A cascade writes CHANGELOG, HOP addendum, EDIT_LOG,
    MEM, Chronicle — not in a single atomic operation. A naive
    "Chronicle must equal CHANGELOG mtime" check false-positives during
    an in-progress cascade. Grace periods (R26: 10min, R50: 5min, R49:
    15min) absorb intra-cascade skew without hiding actual drift.
  • Why hop_open.py is separate from freshness.py. Separation of concerns:
    freshness.py is the authoritative drift checker, standalone and
    importable. hop_open.py is the session-open orchestration, which
    invokes freshness.py as one of its six steps. Other cascade scripts
    (cascade-close, pre-commit, CI) can invoke freshness.py directly
    without depending on the hop-open sequence.

SELF-JUSTIFICATION ON FIRST RUN:
  First execution of freshness.py immediately caught real drift:
  ACTIVE_ANCHORS.md was older than EPISODIC_MEMORY.json — stale from
  MEM-149 and MEM-150 additions without a re-run of anchors.py. Fix:
  python3 sadp/anchors.py. Then all eight checks green. The tool
  validated itself before anyone had to write a test for it.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:
  • Considered embedding freshness checks in hop_updater.py itself.
    Rejected — hop_updater has a single job (regen HOP header). Conflating
    it with drift detection would entangle responsibilities and make
    failures harder to localize.
  • Considered git-hook-based enforcement (pre-commit). Deferred — git
    workflows in this project are operator-driven and inconsistent across
    sessions; binding enforcement to a specific git configuration adds a
    fragile dependency. Python-script-based enforcement runs anywhere
    Python runs.

KEY INSIGHT:
  Drift from omission is a silent failure mode. The omitting cascade
  feels complete to whoever wrote it; the omission is visible only by
  inspection of what did NOT happen. Exhortation cannot close this class
  — an unread warning does nothing. A check that runs unconditionally
  and blocks proceeding does. The difference between "rule declared" and
  "rule enforced" is whether a mechanism exists that refuses to continue
  when the rule is violated.

  R62 FRG is the first rule in the project whose text IS the check
  function. Its enforcement mechanism ships with its definition. New
  rules added after R62 should consider doing the same: if the rule
  describes an invariant, write the check; if the check can run as a
  cascade gate, register it; if it cannot, document why in the rule's
  reason field.

CHRONICLE END (Session 18 — R62 FRG infrastructure close, April 21)

SESSION: 2026-04-21 (Session 18, continuing — declarative checklist)
VERSIONS: Acervator 3.13.7 (no bump) / SADP 1.18
TITLE: From Freshness Checks to Declarative Invariant Table
================================================================================

The R62 FRG rule born a turn earlier (MEM-151) used hand-written Python
functions — one per check. Workable for eight, unmaintainable at thirty.
The operator's directive generalized the pattern:

  "Any rule that calls for file checks should verify date / time
   alignment i.e. update all documents based on their last modified
   date / time and maintain a full checklist that exists in a loop."

WHAT WAS BUILT:
  • sadp/CHECKLIST.json — declarative table. 13 initial invariants.
    Each row: id, rule, description, kind, source/target paths,
    grace_sec, auto_fix command, blocks_cascade flag, plus running
    state (last_status, last_checked, pass_streak, failure_count).
    Adding a new invariant of the common kinds = one JSON row.
  • sadp/checklist.py — data-driven runner. Dispatches by kind
    (mtime_gte, byte_identical, version_match, custom). --self-heal
    runs auto_fix commands. --loop cycles with sleep until clean or
    no fixable failures remain. State persisted back to JSON.
  • sadp/CHECKLIST.md — human-readable dashboard auto-regenerated
    after every run. Group-by-rule tables with status glyphs and
    streak counters; failing items get expanded diagnostic blocks.
  • R62 FRG spec text in SPEC-CORE.md — authored in response to
    the checklist itself flagging its absence (see below).

KEY DECISIONS & RATIONALE:
  • Why declarative. Freshness.py from the previous turn had each
    check as a Python function. That scales to ~ten; beyond that,
    every new rule means a code edit, a function import, and a
    mental model of where it fits. Declarative JSON reduces the
    add-new-invariant cost to one row. Most SADP rules that care
    about file-update alignment fit one of three kinds; only the
    bespoke cases (HOP header parsing, rule-registry integrity)
    remain as Python handlers.
  • Why state persistence. An invariant that flaps — passes, fails,
    passes, fails — suggests either the check is mis-defined or a
    process is writing the file sometimes and not other times.
    failure_count and pass_streak make that visible without adding
    instrumentation. Drift becomes observable in history, not just
    at the current instant.
  • Why blocks_cascade. PM-generator version drift is a real
    warning but should not halt a cascade that doesn't touch the
    PM. Chronicle drift is always a hard stop. The flag lets
    severity match impact without over-blocking.
  • Why auto-fix only on safe items. Chronicle freshness cannot be
    auto-fixed because the Chronicle is narrative — only a human
    knows what to write. R51 version match cannot be auto-fixed
    because the script cannot decide which file has the right
    version. But anchors regeneration, HOP header regeneration,
    and Chronicle copy sync are pure mechanical operations; the
    tool runs them. 6 of 13 items have auto_fix; 7 are human-only.
  • Why --loop. Operator requested a checklist "that exists in a
    loop." The loop runs run_once, checks whether progress is
    possible (any fixable failure?), and either cycles or halts.
    Prevents infinite loops on un-fixable drift while giving the
    self-healing items as many cycles as they need.

SELF-JUSTIFICATION (AGAIN):
  First run of checklist.py immediately caught two real drift
  instances:
    (1) ACTIVE_ANCHORS.md was stale from the previous MEM additions
        — resolved by --self-heal invoking anchors.py.
    (2) SPEC-CORE.md was 3h33m older than RULE_REGISTRY.json — the
        R62 rule was registered in the registry during the previous
        turn but the spec text was never authored. Resolution: this
        very entry, which the tool demanded as a condition of
        proceeding. The rule required its own documentation to
        exist before passing.
  This is the pattern MEM-135 named (HOP header drift → hop_updater)
  and MEM-151 instantiated (R62 FRG → freshness.py). The tool
  justifies its own existence on its first execution every time,
  because drift accumulates faster than it is inspected.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:
  • Considered embedding auto-fix commands as Python functions
    imported from modules. Rejected — shell commands in JSON are
    portable, grep-able, and operator-readable. The tradeoff is
    no type-checking of the command; acceptable because the
    command surfaces its own errors on failure and those surface
    via the subprocess capture.
  • Considered deprecating freshness.py. Left in place for
    backward-compat — external scripts may import it. Marked
    superseded in comment header.

KEY INSIGHT:
  Rules that can be represented as data are more durable than
  rules that can only be represented as code. Data survives
  refactors, can be inspected without running it, and can be
  modified without a code review process. The 13 current rows in
  CHECKLIST.json encode ~80% of the known file-alignment
  invariants in the project. Adding row 14 will be cheaper than
  the previous 13 combined.

  R62 FRG is now implemented at two levels: the CHECK_REGISTRY
  pattern (freshness.py, list of functions — supersedeed) and the
  CHECKLIST.json pattern (data-driven rows, current). The pattern
  lesson is to let operator directives shape the data model, not
  the code model — the operator reasons about "a table of things
  to verify," not "a list of functions."

CHRONICLE END (Session 18 — checklist generalization, April 21)

SESSION: 2026-04-21 (Session 18, continuing — artifact lifecycle)
VERSIONS: Acervator 3.13.7 (no bump) / SADP 1.18
TITLE: Context Bloat Prevention — Declarative Artifact Lifecycle
================================================================================

Operator noticed that /mnt/user-data/outputs/ had accumulated 17 files
and 24 MB across the session — most of it superseded by the session-close
zip. The ask: auto-delete once referenced, regenerate on demand via a
dependency flag.

WHAT WAS BUILT:
  • sadp/ARTIFACTS.json — declarative manifest of 13 artifact patterns
    with lifecycle metadata. Six policies: persistent, current_version_only,
    current_handoff_only, superseded_by_newer, ephemeral, regenerable.
    Each entry has optional regen_command (shell invocation to recreate)
    and depends_on (source files whose change invalidates the artifact).
    Adding a new artifact to the system is one JSON row.
  • sadp/cleanup_outputs.py — three-mode tool. --dry-run reports what
    would be deleted with lifecycle-policy reasons. --apply deletes and
    logs each action to EDIT_LOG. --regen <hint> looks up pattern in
    manifest and runs regen_command to recreate. The regen mechanic IS
    the operator's "dependency flag" — Claude can summon back any
    regenerable artifact without manual work.
  • CHK-014 new checklist invariant — outputs_classification_clean.
    Walks outputs directory, fails if any file matches no ARTIFACTS.json
    pattern. Non-blocking (operator reviews). Prevents silent
    accumulation of bloat going forward.

FIRST APPLY:
  Classified 17 files. 6 KEEP (current PM, handoff zip, tip jar,
  current battery results, current audit inventory — 2.5 MB). 7 STALE
  ephemeral (old review docs, design previews, transient reports —
  190 KB). 3 SUPERSEDED (component zips rolled into the handoff —
  21 MB). Applied cleanup: 17 files → 6 files, 24 MB → 2.5 MB,
  reclaimed 21.3 MB.

KEY DECISIONS & RATIONALE:
  • Why declarative manifest vs hardcoded. Same reason CHECKLIST.json
    is declarative: adding a new artifact should be a data edit, not
    a code edit. Operator can see at a glance what's shipping and why.
  • Why fnmatch glob patterns. Human-readable, matches operator mental
    model ("the PM file" → acervator_product_manual_v*.pdf), and avoids
    the regex-footgun.
  • Why regen_command as shell rather than Python function. Shell
    commands are the common denominator for output-producing tools
    (reportlab runs via python3, but zip is a shell tool, and file
    operations are inherently shell-shaped). JSON holds strings
    portably; Python would require imports.
  • Why the first regen attempt failed. The command used
    `date +%d%m%Y` assuming "today," but the battery data files are
    dated 20042026 — an earlier date. Fixed by extracting the date
    from the MASTER_SUMMARY filename via ls+grep rather than the
    runtime clock. Teaches a pattern: regen commands should derive
    date/version from existing canonical files, not from the wall
    clock. The wall clock will always diverge from the data-file
    date eventually.
  • Why ephemeral vs regenerable distinction. Ephemeral artifacts
    (one-off design previews, transient reports from rule births)
    have no source to regenerate from — they were authored once and
    their content is now in MEM entries or the Chronicle. Deleting
    them is final. Regenerable artifacts (portfolio charts zip, PM)
    have deterministic regen paths; deleting them is reversible.
    The manifest encodes which is which.

SELF-JUSTIFICATION PATTERN — FOURTH INSTANCE:
  Every structural enforcement tool in this project has justified
  itself on first run by catching real drift:
    • MEM-135: hop_updater.py caught 26-addendum header drift
    • MEM-151: freshness.py caught stale ACTIVE_ANCHORS.md
    • MEM-152: checklist.py caught stale SPEC-CORE.md
    • MEM-153: cleanup_outputs.py caught 10 files / 21.3 MB of bloat
  Drift accumulates faster than it is inspected. The fix is always
  the same: automate the inspection. Every new tool in this class
  will earn its keep on day one.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:
  • Considered auto-delete on every session close without operator
    confirmation. Rejected — unknown files get "flag" policy, never
    silent deletion. If a new artifact lands without a manifest
    entry, the checklist complains and the operator decides.
  • Considered content-hashing the depends_on files to avoid
    regenerating when sources haven't changed. Deferred — current
    regen commands are fast (<2s), so the optimization isn't worth
    the bookkeeping yet. If regen times grow (PM generation at
    large sizes), this becomes the next increment.

KEY INSIGHT:
  Context bloat isn't a storage problem. It's a discovery problem:
  more files means more cognitive load deciding which to reference.
  A handoff zip that subsumes 10 component zips is the same
  information in one place; the deletion of the 10 isn't data loss,
  it's noise reduction. The manifest makes that judgment explicit:
  superseded_by_newer encodes "this file's content is also in that
  other file." Once that relationship is declarative, pruning is
  mechanical.

  The declarative-table pattern applied here is the same pattern
  from CHECKLIST.json (MEM-152) and RULE_REGISTRY.json (older):
  data for the what, Python for the how. Three instances is enough
  to call it doctrine: for any future SADP system the operator
  proposes, the default design should be "table of rows with
  policy metadata" before "function per case."

CHRONICLE END (Session 18 — artifact lifecycle, April 21)

================================================================================

WHAT WAS BUILT:

  • Session 19 empirical evidence cited: MEM-154 NEGATIVE RESULTS section
    already documented that the P5 sweep consumed two full turns plus

    in this same edit. Rule-count drift in the README header is the kind
    of thing CHK-015 candidate (narrative-doc freshness, noted in the
    Session 19 HOP addendum) would catch.

  • Why commit R64 before R63. R63 is the meta-rule about external-
    resource-grounding for SADP augmentations. R64 is the immediate
    unblock for the operator's rate-limit pain. R64 can be drafted

    the principle to R64's own drafting (fetched external references,
    cited operator directive, cited Session 19 evidence). R64 first

REGRESSIONS CAUGHT:
  None this turn — no code touched.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:
  None this turn — cascade completed within ceilings, R64 self-applied

KEY INSIGHT:
  The structural enforcement stack (R62 FRG / CHECKLIST / anchors /
  hop_updater / ARTIFACTS) was designed to catch drift at cascade close
  OR hop open. When a cascade-close step is omitted, drift surfaces at

SESSION: 2026-04-21 (Session 20 Addendum 2 — R63 ERG rule birth)
VERSIONS: Acervator 3.13.7 (unchanged) / SADP 1.19 → 1.20 (rule addition)
TITLE: External Resource Grounding — SADP Becomes a Library, Not a Sketchpad
================================================================================

Second Session 20 cascade. Operator approved R63 draft with the specific
disposition "approve, but fetch WP:V + WP:NOR text first" — applying R63's
own principle to its drafting as the acceptance condition. Fetched the
Wikipedia Verifiability and Core Content Policies pages, cited two quotes
(one per source, under 15 words each) confirming the governance-corpus
analogue, committed same chunk.

WHAT WAS BUILT:

  • R63 ERG — External Resource Grounding rule committed. Mental model:
    SADP is a consumed governance resource, not Claude's authoring
    workspace. Rule: every augmentation to SADP artifacts (new rules,
    new ADRs, new SPEC-CORE sections, amendments, new CHECKLIST
    invariants, new workflow docs) MUST cite at least one external
    canonical source in a dedicated "Sources" block. Scope explicitly
    in (SPEC-CORE / RULE_REGISTRY / ADR / CHECKLIST / narrative process
    docs). Scope explicitly out (MEM / EDIT_LOG / Chronicle / CHANGELOG
    / src code / non-substantive edits). Five canonical source classes
    enumerated (operator directive, standards, SE literature, dependency
    docs, prior artifacts). Not-accepted list closes the loophole of
    "appeals to authority without source" and "Claude's reasoning based
    on context is not a source — reasoning is derivation, not source."

  • Observation+framework pattern documented: when a rule is motivated
    by an observed pattern in the project (like R61 CBF born from 18
    silent-swallow sites), the proposal MUST cite BOTH specific MEM/
    EDIT_LOG windows documenting the pattern AND at least one external
    framework naming the failure class. Observation alone is evidence
    that a problem exists; the rule's structure must derive from canon.

  • External grounding for R63 itself was the acceptance test. Eight
    distinct citations: operator directive verbatim; Wikipedia WP:V
    with quote "threshold for inclusion is verifiability, not truth";
    Wikipedia WP:NOR / Core Content Policies with quote "all material
    in Wikipedia must be attributable to a reliable, published source";
    Royal Society motto Nullius in verba (1660); IEEE 29148:2018
    traceability (already in SRS §1.4); internal SADP lineage R40 LTMQ
    / R46 MLHCI / R47 FACP / R49 MDEL; Session 19 empirical evidence
    (MEM-149, MEM-154) where ADR-012 / SRS rewrite / RISK_REGISTER
    additions / ARCHITECTURE rewrite were all authored without external
    grounding — the sketchpad posture operator named; R64 FCP first
    chunk this session as prototype application of the principle R63
    codifies.

KEY DECISIONS & RATIONALE:

  • Why operator required the fetch first. Without fetching the actual
    source text, I'd be citing WP:V and WP:NOR by common knowledge —
    which is the exact "Claude's reasoning based on context is not a
    source" anti-pattern R63 forbids. The fetch is the proof-of-work
    that R63 isn't aspirational; it's operational from the first
    commit. Operator caught this correctly.

  • Why one quote per source under 15 words. Copyright compliance
    (quotes ≥15 words or multiple quotes from one source are severe
    violations per instructions). For R63's purposes, one quote per
    source is plenty — the citation URL carries the full context.

  • Why R63 depends on R64 rather than being standalone. R64's chunking
    workflow is HOW R63 operates at the tactical level — draft, present,
    await approval, commit. Without R64 establishing the turn-level
    discipline, R63 would have no workflow to attach to. R63 is the
    WHAT; R64 is the HOW.

  • Why the GUI design rules task (original Task 1 from Session 20
    opening) is now gated on R63 compliance. Good — that's R63 working
    as designed. Operator picks canonical source(s), Claude fetches
    and cites, drafts with Sources block, operator approves, commit.
    The task becomes properly bounded rather than open-ended "let
    Claude invent GUI rules."

  • Why CHK-017 is deferred to candidate status rather than codified
    now. Pattern-match discipline: structural enforcement works best
    after 2-3 instances establish the citation-block shape. R63 and
    R64 are instances 1 and 2. One more rule addition with a Sources
    block and the shape is clear enough to automate.

REGRESSIONS CAUGHT:
  None this turn — no code touched.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:
  None this turn — cascade completed within R64 ceilings, both rules
  self-applied successfully.

KEY INSIGHT:
  Sessions 17-19 produced a lot of SADP content — rules, ADRs, audit
  docs, meta-docs about meta-docs. Most of it was authored from my
  own reasoning about what seemed like good practice for the project.
  Operator read the cumulative posture as "Claude treating SADP as his
  creative canvas." That read is correct. R63 corrects the posture by
  constraining the authoring process, not by reviewing individual
  outputs. The difference matters: reviewing each ADR individually
  scales linearly with AI output volume (which is increasing); the
  process constraint scales as a per-augmentation check regardless
  of how many augmentations are in flight. That's the same logic
  that made R62 FRG structural rather than textual — textual
  discipline decays; structural discipline holds.

CHRONICLE END (Session 20 Addendum 2 — R63 ERG rule birth, April 21)

SESSION: 2026-04-21 (Session 20 Addendum 3 — R65 GDG rule birth)
VERSIONS: Acervator 3.13.7 (unchanged) / SADP 1.20 → 1.21 (rule addition)
TITLE: GUI Design Grounding — First R63-Compliant Multi-Source Rule
================================================================================

Third Session 20 cascade. Third task from session opening. Operator
requested GUI design rules via Task 1; R63 ERG (committed Addendum 2)
then required operator to select canonical sources before drafting.
Interactive multi_select returned all four candidates chosen (Nielsen +
WCAG + KDE HIG + Material Design 3). Fetched each source, drafted R65
with per-source governing scope and precedence hierarchy, operator
approved as-is, committed same chunk.

WHAT WAS BUILT:

  • R65 GDG — GUI Design Grounding rule committed. Scope in: new
    widgets / dialogs / tabs / layouts / themes in src/gui/, theme
    changes in theme_engine.py, icon changes, keyboard shortcut changes,
    new user-facing GUI text. Scope out: backend code, non-visible
    helpers, minor bug fixes, CLI paths, Product Manual typography.

  • Four canonical sources, each with governing scope:
    - WCAG 2.2 Level AA is the non-negotiable accessibility floor.
      Contrast ratios, keyboard operability, focus indicators, target
      size, error identification not solely by color. Cyberpunk dark
      theme is a design choice; WCAG compliance within that theme is
      a requirement.
    - Nielsen's 10 heuristics are the review checklist at merge time.
      #1 (Visibility of System Status) and #9 (Recognize/Diagnose/
      Recover from Errors) are mandatory gates; the other eight are
      review-advisory.
    - KDE HIG is the primary Qt-native pattern reference — component
      patterns, menu structure, shortcut conventions, settings dialogs.
    - Material Design 3 is the visual-ideas source, adapted not copied.
      Concepts (color tokens, elevation, motion timing, typography
      scale) applied to Qt widgets; the M3 component library is NOT
      imported.

  • Precedence hierarchy codified for when sources conflict: WCAG >
    operator override > KDE HIG (for Qt patterns) > M3 (for visual
    hierarchy where KDE HIG is silent) > Nielsen (review-time criteria
    rather than implementation resolvers).

  • Bridge to code-level rules documented. R28 FL (Fail Loudly) is
    the code-level expression of Nielsen heuristic #1 (Visibility of
    System Status) — if the system hides its state, the UX fails. R61
    CBF (Callback Boundary Fail-Loudly) is the code-level expression
    of Nielsen heuristic #9 (Recognize/Diagnose/Recover from Errors) —
    silent swallows mean users can't recognize or recover. R65 makes
    explicit the governance-to-UX thread that was previously implicit.

KEY DECISIONS & RATIONALE:

  • Why four sources instead of one. Operator selected all four via
    multi_select. Each covers a decision class the others don't: WCAG
    is accessibility enforcement, Nielsen is review criteria, KDE HIG
    is Qt pattern matching, M3 is visual language. Using just one
    would leave three decision classes unsourced. R65's precedence
    hierarchy handles the conflicts that arise from having all four.

  • Why WCAG AA not AAA. AAA is aspirational — even W3C doesn't
    require it for conformance in most contexts. AA is the common
    legal and practical floor. R65 can be amended to require AAA on
    specific components in the future if operator directs.

  • Why M3 components are not imported. Acervator is Qt desktop, not
    Android mobile. M3's component library is designed for Android's
    View system or Flutter or Compose, not for PySide6. Forcing
    component imports would be impedance-mismatch nightmare. Adapting
    M3 concepts (color tokens, elevation semantics, motion timing)
    to Qt widgets gives us the design clarity without the platform
    mismatch.

  • Why Nielsen #1 and #9 are promoted to mandatory gates. Pattern
    match with the project's history: Session 18 documented four
    silent-swallow regressions traced to callback boundaries, each
    producing blind UIs (no status visibility, no error recovery).
    These are Nielsen #1 and #9 failures expressed at the code level.
    Flagging them as mandatory in GUI review catches the UX
    equivalent of R28/R61 violations before they land.

  • Why the existing cyberpunk theme isn't audited in this chunk.
    R65 is the rule; auditing an existing artifact against a
    newly-committed rule is a separate action (per R64 chunking —
    one reviewable unit per chunk). Operator directive would scope
    that audit if they want it done.

REGRESSIONS CAUGHT:
  None this turn — no code touched.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:
  None this turn — cascade completed within ceilings.

KEY INSIGHT:
  R65 is the first SADP rule authored under the R63 discipline with
  genuine multi-source external grounding — five distinct canonical
  URLs in the Sources block, plus internal project precedent. The
  shape of its grounding block is the prototype for future rule
  proposals. Previous rules (R60, R61, R62, R64) had grounding but
  authored before R63 codification; R63 itself was a meta-rule
  bootstrapping the discipline. R65 is the first substantive
  domain-specific rule that demonstrates R63 working at steady state:
  operator picks sources, Claude fetches, Claude cites in the draft,
  operator approves, commit preserves the citations. The pattern
  works; R63 is operational, not aspirational.

CHRONICLE END (Session 20 Addendum 3 — R65 GDG rule birth, April 21)

TITLE: Orientation as First-Class Discipline — Capping Claude's Ceremony

Fourth Session 20 cascade. Operator-requested Task 3 from session opening:

WHAT WAS BUILT:

  • HOP audit measured the real latency class. The hop_open.py script
    runs in 414 ms average across 3 runs (399/431/412 ms). The checklist
    alone is 240 ms. anchors.py is 117 ms. hop_updater.py is 165 ms.
    None of these is the "EXTREMELY long time" the operator flagged.
    The actual source is Claude's historical orientation ceremony —
    running hop_open, then viewing NEXT_SESSION_ORDERS to "confirm,"
    then listing files, then reading the last MEM for detail, then
    re-reading ARCHITECTURE for context, then tailing EDIT_LOG to see
    what happened. 3-8 tool calls before the first response, each with
    its own Claude-side latency, adds up to 15-60 seconds of wall
    clock before orientation is "done."

  • R66 HOD committed. Rule: on --proceed or --query, orientation is
    one bash call. If READY, zero additional reads before first
    response. If BLOCKED, verbatim output + stop. The script's output
    IS the orientation — re-reading summarized files is forbidden.
    Scope exempts default mode (where Claude awaits directive), mid-
    session work, hop_open debugging, and fresh-extraction setup.

  • Audit documented five more findings beyond Finding 1. Finding 3
    (cascade-close holes) is particularly actionable: every auto_fix
    entry in CHECKLIST.json is by definition a hole in ORDER 5.5.
    If the close cascade regenerated the file, the check would always
    pass and self-heal would never run. Every self-heal execution at
    hop-open is evidence that the prior session's close was incomplete.
    The fix is symmetric: for every auto_fix field, add a corresponding
    step to ORDER 5.5. This is Fix #2, pending.

KEY DECISIONS & RATIONALE:

  • Why make R66 a rule vs ORDER 0 amendment. Operator had a button
    option for ORDER 0 amendment and did not choose it. R60 / R64 /
    R66 are all behavioral rules that live in the registry because
    they govern Claude's turn-level decisions, not file-level
    cascade steps. Keeping them in RULE_REGISTRY makes them visible
    to future sessions during SADP orientation via hop_open Step 1.

  • Why MEM-158 combines audit + R66. The audit's Finding 1 IS R66's
    reason for existing. Splitting into two MEM entries would have
    either duplicated content or left R66 with a thin reason field.
    One MEM captures both durably.

  • Why not auto-apply all six fixes this turn. R64. Even though the
    operator approved the full list, "full list" under R64 means
    "sequence of chunks, one at a time," not "batch them all."
    R66 is fix #1; fixes 2-6 await their own chunks.

  • Why R66's own commit is a legitimate R66 exemption. Mid-session
    work for operator-directed task is explicitly scope-excluded. R66
    governs --proceed and --query orientation only, not cascade
    commits mid-session. No conflict.

REGRESSIONS CAUGHT:
  None this turn — no code touched. But Finding 2c (hop_open.py:201
  latent ver.group(1) NameError) is a latent bug flagged for Fix #3.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:
  None this turn.

KEY INSIGHT:
  The gap between "how fast is the script" and "how fast does the
  session actually start" is entirely Claude-side ceremony. The script
  designers (Session 18) did their job; what was missing was a rule
  telling Claude to USE the script's output rather than recapitulating
  its inputs. R66 closes that gap.

  Generalizing: whenever a structural tool produces a summary, there's
  always a risk that Claude re-reads the sources "for context" rather
  than trusting the summary. That pattern has appeared in other places
  too — reading individual MEM entries instead of ACTIVE_ANCHORS,
  reading the full RULE_REGISTRY instead of the hop_open output's
  rule summary, reading the full CHANGELOG instead of the current
  version line. R66's principle — trust the summary, read sources only
  for operator-directed work — might generalize into a broader rule
  later. Not this session.

CHRONICLE END (Session 20 Addendum 4 — HOP Audit + R66 HOD, April 21)

SESSION: 2026-04-21 (Session 20 Addendum 5 — ORDER 5.5 cascade amendment)
VERSIONS: Acervator 3.13.7 (unchanged) / SADP 1.22 (unchanged)
TITLE: Closing the Auto-Fix Hole — Cascade as Inverse of Self-Heal Table
================================================================================

Fifth Session 20 cascade. Fix #2 of 6 from HOP orientation audit.
Process doc tightening, not new capability, so no version bump.

WHAT WAS BUILT:

  • sadp/NEXT_SESSION_ORDERS.md ORDER 5.5 cascade checklist amended.
    Two previously-implicit steps promoted to explicit lines:
    'cp DEVELOPMENT_CHRONICLE.md sadp/DEVELOPMENT_CHRONICLE.md'
    (was buried as sub-bullet under Chronicle append) and
    'python3 sadp/anchors.py' (not in the cascade at all previously,
    despite being the auto_fix for CHK-005 since MEM-151). Also
    added tabular mapping of every current CHECKLIST auto_fix entry
    to its corresponding cascade line, and codified the invariant
    that the auto_fix table IS the inverse of the cascade — every
    CHK with an auto_fix implies a cascade step.

  • checklist.py promoted in the cascade text to 'final verification
    gate' framing. Previously it was just another line item; now it's
    positioned as the terminal check that runs after all regens.

KEY DECISIONS & RATIONALE:

  • Why not bump SADP version. The auto_fix commands already existed
    in CHECKLIST.json. The cascade commands already existed at the
    operational level (Session 20's prior chunks have been running
    anchors.py in-cascade since R64's commit). This amendment just
    makes what was operationally true doctrinally explicit. No new
    capability was added. If a future session reads ORDER 5.5, they
    now see all three regen steps; previously they'd have discovered
    anchors.py only via hop-open self-heal.

  • Why also add the tabular auto_fix->cascade mapping. The mapping
    IS the invariant that prevents future drift. When someone adds
    CHK-019 with an auto_fix, the table needs a new row, which forces
    them to also add the cascade step. Without the table, the auto_fix
    could land without a corresponding cascade step, and we'd be back
    to discovering-via-self-heal.

  • Why not batch fix #3 (NameError patch) with this amendment.
    Operator chose single-chunk mode ('Fix #2 alone'). R64 chunking.
    The NameError is a one-liner and could fit, but respecting the
    operator's chunk choice is more important than saving a turn.

REGRESSIONS CAUGHT:
  The HOP audit itself found this hole and fixed it. No new regressions
  surfaced by the amendment.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:
  None this turn.

KEY INSIGHT:
  Every auto_fix command in a checklist is documentation of a hole.
  The checklist says 'X must be true'; the auto_fix says 'if X isn't
  true, here's how to make it true.' If the close cascade makes X
  true at close, the auto_fix never fires. Therefore: for every
  auto_fix, there should be an exactly-corresponding close-cascade
  step. The cascade and the auto_fix table are duals of each other.

  This is a generalizable pattern for any structural-enforcement
  system that also has self-heal: the enforcement table and the
  generation table should be inverses. If self-heal ever runs, that's
  evidence the generation table is incomplete. Useful lens for future
  SADP design.

CHRONICLE END (Session 20 Addendum 5 — ORDER 5.5 amendment, April 21)

SESSION: 2026-04-21 (Session 20 Addendum 6 — ARTIFACTS manifest extension)
VERSIONS: Acervator 3.13.7 (unchanged) / SADP 1.22 (unchanged)
TITLE: Classifying the Unclassified — One JSON Row, Two Warnings Gone
================================================================================

Sixth Session 20 cascade. Fix #6 of 6 from HOP audit. Smallest landing
in the fix list.

WHAT WAS BUILT:

  • sadp/ARTIFACTS.json artifacts[] array gained one row: pattern
    session*_*.md, lifecycle ephemeral, keep false. Generalized to
    match any future session's individual-file deliverables, not
    just Session 19's specific files. Rationale documents that content
    is redundant with the session-close handoff zip.

  • Effect: CHK-014 perpetual warnings on session19_*.md files
    resolved. Files remain on disk (not this chunk's job to delete)
    but are now classified. Next cleanup_outputs.py --apply will
    remove them per ephemeral policy.

KEY DECISIONS & RATIONALE:

  • Why ephemeral vs superseded_by_newer. Superseded_by_newer in the
    ARTIFACTS schema means older-instances-of-same-pattern are
    pruned when newer-instances-of-same-pattern exist. That's for
    things like portfolio_charts_DATE.zip where Session 20's newer
    zip supersedes Session 19's older zip. The session19_*.md files
    aren't superseded by session20_*.md files — they're superseded
    by the session19 handoff zip, a different pattern. Ephemeral
    captures 'safe to delete, content is elsewhere' accurately.

  • Why not also delete the files this chunk. Operator asked for
    'ARTIFACTS pattern' specifically. Deleting files is a separate
    action that should be intentional, not bundled. The pattern
    addition tells cleanup_outputs.py what to do; running cleanup
    is the next, separate action.

  • Why generalize to session*_*.md vs specific session19_*.md.
    The generic pattern covers all future sessions including this
    one. Specific would require updating the manifest every session.
    Manifest should be pattern-based, not instance-based.

REGRESSIONS CAUGHT:
  None.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:
  None.

KEY INSIGHT:
  The ARTIFACTS manifest is a classifier for /mnt/user-data/outputs/
  content. Any persistent warning from CHK-014 means a class of
  artifact hasn't been taught to the classifier yet. This is the
  second time the manifest has been extended for a recurring warning
  class (previous time was the initial 13-pattern manifest, MEM-153).
  Each extension is educational about what patterns the project
  actually produces. Over time the manifest converges to comprehensive.

CHRONICLE END (Session 20 Addendum 6 — ARTIFACTS extension, April 21)

SESSION: 2026-04-21 (Session 20 Addendum 7 — ADR pattern orphan resolution)
VERSIONS: Acervator 3.13.7 (unchanged) / SADP 1.22 (unchanged)
TITLE: Closing the Last Orphan — Generic Over Specific in Manifest Patterns
================================================================================

Seventh Session 20 cascade. Follow-up to Addendum 6. The session*_*.md
pattern resolved two of three Session 19 outputs-dir orphans; ADR-012-
callback-boundary-fail-loudly.md didn't match because it lacked the
session19_ prefix. This chunk adds an ADR-*.md ephemeral pattern to
close the last CHK-014 warning.

WHAT WAS BUILT:

  • sadp/ARTIFACTS.json artifacts[] array gained one row: pattern
    ADR-*.md, lifecycle ephemeral, keep false. Rationale documents
    that canonical ADR copy lives in docs/adr/ within the repo,
    so outputs-dir presence is presentation-only and redundant with
    the session-close handoff zip.

KEY DECISIONS & RATIONALE:

  • Why a generic ADR-*.md pattern vs specific ADR-012-*. Generic
    future-proofs — any future session presenting a new ADR via
    outputs will match without manifest updates. Specific would
    require manifest extension every ADR landing. Manifest should
    be pattern-based, not instance-based. Same reasoning as
    Addendum 6's session*_*.md generalization.

  • Why Session 19 presented the ADR via outputs in the first place.
    Checking chronologically: Session 19's P5 sweep produced a
    net-new ADR-012 and the operator requested individual-file
    presentation alongside the close zip. Presentation convention
    in that session named individual files session19_<name>.md for
    refreshed docs BUT the net-new ADR kept its canonical filename
    to avoid confusion — Session 19 wasn't authoring a new session-
    prefix convention for the ADR that had its own permanent name.
    Reasonable call at the time; left an outputs-dir orphan that
    the manifest now covers.

REGRESSIONS CAUGHT:
  None.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:
  None. But this is the second time this session the manifest has
  needed extension after an outputs-dir delivery landed outside
  existing patterns. Pattern: whenever a new delivery class lands,
  manifest extension should happen same-chunk.

KEY INSIGHT:
  Addenda 6 and 7 are the same class of fix — both just add a row
  to ARTIFACTS.json to classify what the classifier was missing.
  Every persistent CHK-014 warning is a delivery class the manifest
  hasn't learned yet. A well-tuned manifest converges to zero
  persistent warnings, and that takes a few iterations of
  'surface warning → add pattern' as new delivery types emerge.
  Session 20's three-pattern-extension history (session*_*.md,
  ADR-*.md, and implicit future patterns) is the convergence
  process operating.

SESSION: 2026-04-21 (Session 20 Addendum 8 — hop_open.py rewrite batch)
VERSIONS: Acervator 3.13.7 (unchanged) / SADP 1.22 (unchanged)
TITLE: Closing the HOP Audit — All Six Fixes + Orphan Resolution Shipped
================================================================================

Eighth Session 20 cascade. Final HOP audit fix batch. Operator used
explicit "Batch" button to relax R64's normal one-chunk-per-fix
discipline — all three fixes target hop_open.py, so a single coherent
rewrite is cleaner than three sequential passes at the same file.

WHAT WAS BUILT:

  • sadp/hop_open.py rewritten with three fixes applied in one pass:
    - Fix #3: ver=None initialized before if gen.exists(): block so
      the downstream version-mismatch check can't raise NameError
      when build_product_manual.py is missing.
    - Fix #4a: new _read_code_version() helper called once in main(),
      result passed down to both emit_sadp_summary and emit_product_
      manual. Previously src/__init__.py was read twice, once per
      function, with a risk of mid-execution drift.
    - Fix #4b: emit_product_manual reads only the first 200 lines of
      build_product_manual.py via readline loop. VERSION is in the
      first 30 lines by convention; loading the full 101KB just to
      regex one string was wasteful.
    - Fix #5: new --brief argparse flag. Each emit_* function accepts
      brief: bool = False. In brief mode, banners are skipped and
      each section prints a single compressed summary line. Output
      drops from 124 lines (~9KB) to 11 lines (~1.2KB) — 10x
      compression. Combinable with --query and --proceed.

  • Timing savings measured: default mode 384ms avg (down from 414ms
    baseline — 30ms improvement from cached __init__.py read plus
    the head-only build_product_manual read). Brief mode similar
    timing (the win is output compression, not execution speed).

KEY DECISIONS & RATIONALE:

  • Why a rewrite vs four str_replace operations. Four str_replaces
    would touch four different regions of the file. Cumulative
    complexity and regression risk is higher than one coherent
    rewrite where you can see all the changes together. Rewrite
    used R64's 1-existing-file-rewrite slot cleanly.

  • Why EPISODIC_MEMORY and RULE_REGISTRY were NOT optimized. Tail-
    parsing JSON backward is fragile — you have to find the last
    closing brace, handle nested objects, and worst-case the file
    has trailing whitespace or a BOM and your seek target is wrong.
    For a saving of ~30ms on a local disk, the complexity isn't
    worth it. Documented in MEM-162 so future sessions don't
    re-propose this optimization.

  • Why no SADP version bump. R63/R64/R65/R66 each bumped SADP by
    0.01 for a rule addition. Tooling changes haven't bumped SADP
    this session (the Product Manual regen in prior sessions didn't,
    cleanup_outputs.py didn't). A CLI flag addition is tooling
    ergonomics, not doctrine. Leaving SADP at 1.22 is consistent.

  • Why Fix #5 (--brief) earns its own flag rather than replacing
    default output. Brief mode is a tradeoff: cheaper output at
    the cost of detail. Different sessions and orientation contexts
    want different tradeoffs. First-time session orientation might
    benefit from full output; returning-session mid-day hops benefit
    from brief. Keeping both modes lets each context pick its own
    fit. R66 HOD doesn't mandate one or the other — it mandates
    "one bash call" regardless of which mode.

REGRESSIONS CAUGHT:
  Fix #3 defused a latent bug rather than catching a regression.
  No active regressions surfaced.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:
  None. All four tested modes worked on first rewrite (default,
  --query, --proceed, --brief, and --brief --proceed combined).
  One polish iteration required for brief output: nested parens
  in the SADP summary and a redundant 'primary: ?' line in Orders.
  Both fixed via str_replace before cascade.

KEY INSIGHT:
  HOP audit opened with a measurement: the script runs in 414ms but
  Claude's orientation ceremony extends wall-clock to 15-60s. R66
  capped the ceremony; --brief now caps the output bandwidth. The
  two fixes compose: an R66-disciplined session using --brief
  produces ~1.2KB of orientation output in ~400ms with exactly one
  tool call. That's probably near-optimal without fundamentally
  changing what orientation reports.

  Generalizing: any orchestration tool has two axes to optimize —
  how many tool calls it takes (R66) and how much data each call
  returns (--brief). They're independent. A session is slow if
  either axis is unbounded.

CHRONICLE END (Session 20 Addendum 8 — hop_open.py rewrite, April 21)

SESSION: 2026-04-21 (Session 20 CLOSE)
VERSIONS: Acervator 3.13.7 (unchanged) / SADP 1.18 → 1.22 (four rule bumps)
TITLE: The Governance Session — Four Rules, One Audit, Zero Code
================================================================================

Session 20 close. Session that didn't touch Acervator code at all —
all work happened in the SADP layer. Four rules, one HOP audit with
six fixes, a cascade doc tightening, two manifest extensions, and a
tooling rewrite. Nine addenda to HOP4 across one working day.

ARC OF THE SESSION:

  Session opened with three operator tasks:
  1. Augment SADP with GUI design rules
  2. Forced chunking for long tasks
  3. HOP orientation audit

  The operator's framing for task 1 was critical: "You never augment
  on your own. You go get resources as it is a resource itself. Not
  your sketchpad. Make it a rule." That meta-instruction birthed R63
  ERG before R65 GDG could be written, because R63 is the prerequisite
  discipline for authoring R65 correctly. Task 1 therefore produced
  two rules: the meta (R63) and the concrete GUI rule (R65).

  Task 2 produced R64 FCP, capping per-turn execution grain. R64 was
  committed first (Addendum 1) because it affected how every
  subsequent chunk would be structured.

  Task 3 produced the full HOP audit (Addendum 4 opening) + R66 HOD
  + five implementation fixes: ORDER 5.5 amendment (Addendum 5),
  two ARTIFACTS pattern additions (Addenda 6 and 7), and one
  hop_open.py rewrite (Addendum 8) batching three separate fixes
  with explicit operator 'batch' directive under R64 relaxation.

  Addendum 9 is this session close.

KEY DELIVERABLES:

  • R64 FCP — Forced Chunking Protocol. ≤15 tool calls per turn,
    ≤1 new output file, ≤1 existing file rewritten, ~3000 output
    tokens. Relaxation only by explicit operator statement.
  • R63 ERG — External Resource Grounding. SADP augmentations cite
    ≥1 external canonical source in a Sources block. First rule
    authored under this discipline was R65 (later the same day).
  • R65 GDG — GUI Design Grounding. WCAG 2.2 AA mandatory
    accessibility floor + Nielsen 10 heuristics review checklist
    (#1 and #9 mandatory gates) + KDE HIG Qt-native patterns +
    Material Design 3 visual ideas adapted. Precedence hierarchy
    codified. Bridges to R28 FL (Nielsen #1) and R61 CBF (Nielsen #9).
  • R66 HOD — Hop Orientation Discipline. Exactly 1 bash call on
    --proceed or --query; zero additional reads. Caps historical
    3-8 tool-call orientation overhead at 1.
  • ORDER 5.5 amendment — explicit cp + anchors + hop_updater
    cascade steps. Tabular invariant: auto_fix table = inverse of
    cascade. Every auto_fix command implies a missing cascade step.
  • hop_open.py rewrite — Fix #3 (ver NameError), Fix #4 (cached
    __init__.py read + head-only build_product_manual.py read),
    Fix #5 (--brief mode, 10x output compression). Measured 30ms
    default-mode speedup.
  • Two ARTIFACTS patterns: session*_*.md and ADR-*.md, both
    ephemeral. Resolved CHK-014 perpetual warnings.

KEY DECISIONS & RATIONALE:

  • Why R64 first. It affected every subsequent commit's structure.
    Committing R64 first meant every later chunk was measurably
    disciplined (tool counts logged, file ceilings respected).

  • Why R63 before R65 despite both being Task 1. Operator's meta-
    framing made R63 logically prerequisite. Writing R65 without
    first writing R63 would have been writing a rule that the
    rule-writing protocol itself hadn't been codified for.

  • Why the HOP audit surfaced cascade-close holes. Every auto_fix
    in CHECKLIST.json is evidence that the close cascade missed
    a step. The audit generalized this into the ORDER 5.5 tabular
    invariant — future CHK additions with auto_fix MUST add
    corresponding cascade steps in the same commit.

  • Why hop_open.py rewrite was one chunk not three. Operator
    explicitly said "Batch #3 + #4 + #5 (all hop_open.py edits)".
    Same file, coherent refactor. R64 relaxation logged verbatim
    in MEM-162 per the rule's own relaxation clause.

  • Why no Acervator version bump. Session 20 was process/tooling/
    governance work. No Acervator features changed. No code outside
    the sadp/ directory was modified. 3.13.7 remains the latest
    shipped Acervator version.

  • Why SADP bumped four times (1.18→1.19→1.20→1.21→1.22). Each rule
    addition is a new SADP capability. Other changes (ORDER 5.5
    amendment, ARTIFACTS patterns, hop_open.py rewrite) did not
    bump SADP because they're process or tooling tightenings
    rather than new doctrinal capabilities.

REGRESSIONS CAUGHT:
  Fix #3 defused the hop_open.py:201 latent NameError before it
  bit. No active regressions this session.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:
  None major. Minor: initial --brief mode had nested parens + a
  redundant 'primary: ?' line, both fixed via str_replace polish
  before commit.

KEY INSIGHT:
  This session demonstrates the SADP layer evolving toward
  self-governance. Before Session 20, rule proposals were sometimes
  authored without explicit external grounding (pattern-matched
  from SE literature in Claude's training, not cited). After R63
  ERG, that can't happen silently. R63's first real test was R65
  (same session, same day), and the discipline held: five external

  The HOP audit and its fix cascade show a similar meta-pattern:

SESSION: 2026-04-21 (Session 21 Addendum 1 — RAIntSimBat moved under sadp/)
VERSIONS: Acervator 3.13.7 (unchanged) / SADP 1.22 → 1.23
TITLE: Two Techs, One Tree — Structural Integration of the Simulation Battery
================================================================================

First Session 21 cascade. Operator directive: combine RAIntSimBat and
SADP. Option B selected (move under sadp/) over A (governance hooks
only), C (merge into src/), D (rename concept).

WHAT WAS BUILT:

  • RAIntSimBat/ physically moved to sadp/RAIntSimBat/. This changes
    the project's top-level structure — SADP is no longer just a
    governance directory, it now contains the 259 KB simulation
    engine + its support files (reports_pdf, ab_report, run_all,
    package_run) as first-class subtree.

  • Cross-file paths patched in four files (root wrapper, test,
    version_sweep, demo_verifier). demo_verifier kept legacy path
    candidates as fallbacks — older PyInstaller bundles that still
    have the old layout will still work. This prevents breaking
    frozen builds in the field.

  • ARTIFACTS.json gained 5 patterns covering the RAIntSimBat
    subtree with appropriate lifecycles: reports (superseded_by_
    newer + keep, historical log), PDFs (same), progress/manifest
    transient (ephemeral), data/cache persistent (web-verified OHLCV
    anchors, expensive to rebuild).

KEY DECISIONS & RATIONALE:

  • Why Option B vs A. Option A (governance hooks only, no move)
    would have kept RAIntSimBat/ at root and added invariants to
    track it from a distance. But the operator's framing — "these
    two techs combined... more interrelated than separate" — reads
    as wanting physical integration, not just logical. Option B
    delivers that.

  • Why not Option C (merge into src/). src/ is application code —
    GUI, trading engine, exchange adapters, competition system.
    RAIntSimBat is a simulation battery that validates the trading
    engine, not part of the live application. It belongs adjacent
    to the validation layer (SADP), not inside the validated layer
    (src/).

  • Why retain legacy path fallbacks in demo_verifier. PyInstaller
    bundles created before this change still have the old layout.
    Removing the legacy probes would break those bundles. Keeping
    them costs nothing (failed probes are free) and preserves
    graceful upgrade path.

  • Why defer CHK-015 r42-at-close gate. CHK-015 needs a "custom"
    handler added to checklist.py, plus careful consideration of
    what happens when tests fail (auto_fix? manual? blocking
    always?). That's a focused design decision deserving its own
    chunk per R64. Rushing it here would conflate the move with
    the enforcement.

  • Why bump SADP 1.22→1.23. Structural capability change: SADP's
    physical scope expanded to contain the simulation battery.
    That's new SADP territory, even though no new rule was added.
    Past precedent: rule additions bumped, tooling changes
    didn't. This is between — structural rather than doctrinal,
    but more than cosmetic.

REGRESSIONS CAUGHT:
  One syntax error surfaced during the demo_verifier patch — the
  meipass try-block addition had wrong indentation, breaking the
  except clause. Caught by `python3 -c import` smoke in the
  verification step; fixed via str_replace before commit. This
  exemplifies why R28 FL matters — fail loudly on import error,
  not silently.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:
  None aside from the indentation error. All 4 r42 parity tests
  pass post-move. BTC smoke battery wins. Reports land at new
  path.

KEY INSIGHT:
  The fact that RAIntSimBat used Path(__file__).parent for its
  reports and data/cache paths meant the move required ONLY
  cross-file patches, not internal refactoring. Good path hygiene
  inside the module saved hours of debugging that a brittle-
  relative-paths version would have cost. This is a generalizable
  lesson: modules that internally use __file__-relative paths are
  location-agnostic and can be relocated mechanically. Modules
  that hard-code "project/subdir/foo" paths can't. Worth keeping
  in mind for any future src/ refactor.

  Another observation: the operator's framing "not going to sell
  it, tip jars cover monetization" is a clarifying boundary
  condition. It means structural cleanup can be prioritized over
  "what would customers want to see" — which is a different
  optimization target. Simpler is better when there's no market
  constraint to preserve.

CHRONICLE END (Session 21 Addendum 1 — RAIntSimBat move, April 21)

    module-level test_ functions and test class methods, runs
    each with try/except for AssertionError (test-failure) and
    generic Exception (test-error / infrastructure issue).
    Returns pass/fail tuple with specific failure details.
    Registered in CUSTOM_HANDLERS dict as r42_parity_tests.

  - sadp/CHECKLIST.json gained CHK-015: custom kind, handler
    r42_parity_tests, blocks_cascade true, auto_fix null.
    Rationale field cites the ORDER 5.5 invariant codified
    Session 20 Addendum 5: absence of auto_fix is correct
    because no cascade step makes a failing parity test pass.
    Parity failures are engine drift; they require human
    diagnosis, not regeneration.

KEY DECISIONS AND RATIONALE:

  - Why blocking. R42 Cross-Engine Sync is core doctrine. If
    simulator and RAIntSimBat engines drift, every battery
    result becomes suspect. Blocking at cascade close means
    this drift cannot silently land across sessions. The
    operator retains the ability to override via explicit R60
    directive if an environmental issue causes false failures.

  - Why custom handler vs subprocess pytest. This environment
    doesn't have pytest available (no network for pip install).
    importlib dispatch works around that and enables richer
    error reporting than subprocess exit codes.

  - Why no auto_fix. ORDER 5.5 invariant: auto_fix table is
    the inverse of the cascade. For CHK-015, there is no
    cascade step that makes failing tests pass. The fix is
    to locate the drift in simulator.py or the RAIntSimBat
    engine and mirror the change. Human work, not automation.

  - Why run at every checklist invocation. Simplicity. The
    custom-handler pattern runs at every check-all pass.
    Adding conditional skipping would require framework
    extension. ~2-3s overhead per check is tolerable, and
    running at hop-open too means session-start validates
    the invariant before work begins.

  - Why SADP 1.23 to 1.24. New checklist capability: custom
    handler that runs a test suite. SADP enforcement surface
    is broader. Past precedent: checklist additions (R62 FRG
    itself) bumped SADP.

REGRESSIONS CAUGHT:
  None — CHK-015 verifies R42 holds and R42 did hold both
  before and after this chunk. The first cascade attempt hit
  a heredoc quote-conflict when I embedded a Python triple-
  quoted docstring inside a hop-addition string literal —
  caught on compile, retried with paraphrased content.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:
  Checklist runtime grows roughly 10x: ~240 ms to ~2-3 s per
  invocation. Acceptable cost for structural R42 enforcement.
  Operator can remove CHK-015 if the overhead ever becomes
  problematic, but the parity guarantee would be lost.

KEY INSIGHT:
  This chunk illustrates a generalizable pattern: any standing
  regression test in a codebase can be promoted from ad-hoc
  to structural enforcement by adding a custom CHECKLIST
  handler that runs it at every cascade close. The handler
  function is around 50 lines, the registration is one line,
  the CHECKLIST entry is one JSON object. Cost is small
  runtime overhead at cascade time; benefit is invariant
  enforcement.

  Candidates for future similar promotions: test_silent_
  swallow_audit (R28 FL), test_engine_callback_delivery
  (R61 CBF), test_nuclear_candle_validation (R47 TRLS).
  Each could become a CHK-NNN with minimal incremental cost.
  The trade-off matrix is the same: seconds of runtime vs.
  structural guarantee.

CHRONICLE END (Session 21 Addendum 2 — CHK-015 R42 parity gate)

SESSION: 2026-04-21 (Session 21 Addendum 3 — CHK-016 engine version tracking)
VERSIONS: Acervator 3.13.7 (unchanged) / SADP 1.24 → 1.25
TITLE: One Version, One Declaration — Light-Enforcement First, Tighten Later
================================================================================

Third Session 21 cascade. Second shipment from the deferred items list.
CHK-016 establishes a canonical engine-version declaration for RAInt
SimBat and verifies it's referenced in the engine code. Non-blocking
initially because historical version strings still exist inside
RAIntSimBat.py and reconciling them is separate work.

WHAT WAS BUILT:

  - sadp/RAIntSimBat/ENGINE_VERSION.json created. Schema: engine_
    version (canonical), description, last_updated, compatible_
    acervator_range, notes. Current value v3.1.92 — matches what
    RAIntSimBat.py actually prints at runtime when a battery runs.

  - sadp/checklist.py gained _handler_engine_version_tracking.
    Three checks: manifest file exists and parses; engine_version
    field matches version pattern; declared version string appears
    at least once in RAIntSimBat.py engine source. Registered in
    CUSTOM_HANDLERS as engine_version_tracking.

  - sadp/CHECKLIST.json gained CHK-016: custom kind, handler
    engine_version_tracking, blocks_cascade FALSE (deliberately
    non-blocking for initial landing), auto_fix null.

KEY DECISIONS AND RATIONALE:

  - Why non-blocking first. RAIntSimBat.py has historical version
    strings (v3.9.0 header comment, v3.1.92 accumulation tag, v3.9.10
    in R55 section, v3.2.6 / v3.7.0 historical notes). If CHK-016
    were blocking and any of these strings went stale, every cascade
    would halt. Non-blocking surfaces the invariant without turning
    it into a cascade-stopper before the historical reconciliation
    chunk lands.

  - Why v3.1.92 as the canonical. That's what prints at runtime:
    print_battery_summary receives engine_ver='v3.1.92' from its
    caller. The header comment's v3.9.0 is a historical marker from
    when the documentation-signal-set last bumped. v3.1.92 is the
    functional truth.

  - Why no auto_fix. Per ORDER 5.5 invariant: auto_fix table is
    the inverse of the cascade. For CHK-016, there's no cascade
    step that could regenerate the engine version — that's
    operator-authored doctrine. Null auto_fix is correct.

  - Why 3 checks vs more comprehensive. Each check adds testing
    surface and maintenance cost. The three chosen are the minimum
    that establishes: canonical exists + is sensible + is actually
    referenced. Strengthening (e.g., "ALL version strings match
    canonical") requires first doing the reconciliation chunk.

  - Why SADP 1.24 to 1.25. New checklist capability: version-
    manifest-tracking pattern. Extends SADP's enforcement surface
    with an ENGINE_VERSION.json shape that can be applied to
    other subsystems later (e.g., a future build tools version
    manifest, or the product manual generator version manifest).

REGRESSIONS CAUGHT:
  None. CHK-016 doesn't verify anything was previously broken — it
  establishes a declaration that wasn't there before.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:
  None. Cascade completed within ceilings.

KEY INSIGHT:
  CHK-016 is intentionally a starter invariant. It codifies the
  structural requirement (single canonical declaration) without
  trying to fix all the existing inconsistency in one leap. The
  pattern: ship the structural gate first with permissive mode,
  fix the historical drift in a follow-up chunk, then tighten
  the gate. This is how to add governance to a live system
  without breaking it. Compare with CHK-015 R42 parity which
  could ship blocking immediately because the parity tests
  already passed — there was no backlog of drift to clear first.

  The pattern generalizes: adding structural enforcement to a
  pre-existing codebase requires a three-phase plan — (1) ship
  the enforcement non-blocking, (2) reconcile historical drift,
  (3) promote to blocking. Doing all three in one chunk is risky;
  splitting respects existing state and operator attention budget.

CHRONICLE END (Session 21 Addendum 3 — CHK-016 engine version tracking)

SESSION: 2026-04-21 (Session 21 Addendum 4 — version reconciliation + CHK-016 promoted)
VERSIONS: Acervator 3.13.7 (unchanged) / SADP 1.25 → 1.26
TITLE: Three-Phase Governance — First Complete Demonstration
================================================================================

Fourth Session 21 cascade. Completes the pattern Session 21 Addendum 3
introduced: ship non-blocking, reconcile drift, promote to blocking.
This chunk is phases 2 + 3 combined.

WHAT WAS BUILT:

  - sadp/RAIntSimBat/RAIntSimBat.py had 7 current-state v3.9.0
    claims updated to canonical v3.1.92 via surgical str_replace
    patches. Targets: header comment, fallback __version__ (to
    3.13.7 matching Acervator), run_v3192 docstring, print_
    battery_summary default parameter, extended battery banner,
    and two JSON report output fields.

  - 4 historical markers deliberately preserved: v3.2.6 (offline
    portfolio sim), v3.1.99 (fee tier), v3.7.0 (Ichimoku), and
    v3.9.10 (R55 VH session 18). These describe WHEN features
    landed — accurate history that should remain.

  - sadp/CHECKLIST.json CHK-016 promoted: blocks_cascade false →
    true. Rationale field updated documenting the promotion.

KEY DECISIONS AND RATIONALE:

  - Why fallback __version__ went to 3.13.7 not 3.1.92. The
    fallback is the Acervator application version (used when
    `from src import __version__` fails to import). It's not
    the engine version. Matching Acervator's current version
    is correct behavior for that field.

  - How to distinguish history from current-state in the engine
    code. Rule of thumb: if the string describes WHEN something
    happened, it's history (preserve). If it describes WHAT the
    current state is, it's current-state (reconcile). Examples:
    "Added v3.2.6 to support offline portfolio simulation" is
    WHEN — preserved. "v3.9.0 engine: ATR+RSI signals..." is
    WHAT the engine currently IS — reconciled.

  - Why batch reconciliation + promotion in one chunk. These
    are logically inseparable. You cannot promote CHK-016 safely
    without first reconciling. Splitting into two chunks would
    leave a window where CHK-016's rationale ("promote after
    reconciliation") was stale. Operator's disposition button
    "Reconcile → promote" explicitly grouped them.

  - Why SADP 1.25 to 1.26. Promoting a non-blocking check to
    blocking is a meaningful tightening of the enforcement
    surface — SADP's effective restriction scope grew. Cleaner
    to track with a version bump than to hide it in a minor
    change.

  - Why not promote CHK-016 to also check "no v3.x stale
    strings exist anywhere". That requires distinguishing
    history from current-state at check time, which is the
    hard part. The current 3-point check (file exists + valid
    pattern + referenced in engine) is adequate as a floor.
    Over-engineering the invariant now would delay tightening
    later when needs are clearer.

REGRESSIONS CAUGHT:
  None. R42 parity tests stayed 4/4 throughout. BTC smoke
  battery wins on both pre- and post-change runs. Runtime print
  was already "Engine: v3.1.92" (caller-provided), so no user-
  facing output changed.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:
  Initial audit (Chunk 1) missed the 3 current-state v3.9.0
  claims at lines 3500, 5222, 5371 — I only caught 4 targets
  from my first pass and had to re-grep after the first three
  str_replaces to find the other 3. Lesson: "find all the
  references" requires an exhaustive grep, not a memory-based
  list from the audit. Captured as a process note for future
  reconciliation chunks.

KEY INSIGHT:
  The three-phase governance pattern (ship non-blocking,
  reconcile, promote) is now validated end-to-end. The costs
  were: (a) CHK-016 Addendum 3 — introducing the gate, trivial;
  (b) version reconciliation + promotion here, moderate effort
  (seven surgical patches + verification). The benefit: R42
  Cross-Engine Sync now has structural enforcement of the
  engine-version declaration layer on top of the parity test
  layer (CHK-015). Two invariants, one rule, enforced at
  every cascade. This is what "combining SADP and RAIntSimBat"
  looks like at the structural level.

  A broader lesson: historical references in code are valuable
  documentation and should not be auto-scrubbed. But current-
  state claims should be reconciled when they diverge. The
  distinction is semantic, not syntactic — no regex can tell
  them apart. Human judgment is the disambiguator. Governance
  tooling can catch current-state drift after canonicalization;
  it cannot canonicalize without intent.

CHRONICLE END (Session 21 Addendum 4 — version reconciliation + CHK-016 promotion)

SESSION: 2026-04-21 (Session 21 Addendum 5 — documentation path sweep)
VERSIONS: Acervator 3.13.7 (unchanged) / SADP 1.26 (unchanged)
TITLE: Closing the Visible Drift — 13 Path References Aligned to sadp/
================================================================================

Fifth Session 21 cascade. Cleanup-tier work completing the visible-
state half of the RAIntSimBat-SADP combination. Addenda 1-4 handled
the structural and enforcement layers; this addendum handles the
documentation layer.

WHAT WAS BUILT:

  - 13 RAIntSimBat/ path references updated to sadp/RAIntSimBat/
    across 6 authoritative files: README.md (tree diagram),
    TECH_DEBT.md + sadp/TECH_DEBT.md mirror (code location
    references and historical fix narratives), generate_essay.py
    and src/gui/demo_runner.py (user-facing prose/dialog strings),
    docs/tools/build_product_manual.py (Product Manual narrative).

  - Method: single Python script with targeted .replace() ops,
    context-scoped to match only intended substrings. Verification
    via negative-lookbehind grep: 0 bare path references remain.

KEY DECISIONS AND RATIONALE:

  - Why not update HOP2/3/5 at root. Those are stale historical
    snapshots from earlier hop generations. The living HOP is
    sadp/ACERVATOR_HOP4.md. Touching the stale snapshots to
    change old paths would falsify historical records — they
    describe what was true AT THAT TIME.

  - Why no SADP version bump. Cleanup aligning docs with already-
    landed structural change is not a new capability. Bumping
    SADP here would dilute the version signal (bumps should
    mean something changed in what SADP can do, not what it
    says). Past precedent: docs-only chunks haven't bumped.

  - Why update TECH_DEBT historical fix narratives. TECH_DEBT
    is a living document describing current state for operator
    reference. If a developer opens it to trace the "bundle
    path fix from Hop 4," the paths in the narrative should
    lead to where the code lives now. Historical accuracy of
    past events is preserved in Chronicle and MEM entries, not
    in TECH_DEBT.

  - Why TECH_DEBT root vs sadp mirror didn't need sync. Unlike
    DEVELOPMENT_CHRONICLE.md (which has CHK-003 enforcing byte-
    identity), TECH_DEBT has no mirror invariant. The two copies
    are allowed to diverge. Both got updated independently here
    because both had stale references.

  - Why count scopes were tricky. My first verification script
    counted "RAIntSimBat/" substring occurrences before and
    after, expecting the count to drop. But "sadp/RAIntSimBat/"
    contains "RAIntSimBat/" as a substring, so the count stayed
    the same. Had to re-verify with negative lookbehind to
    distinguish bare references from prefixed ones. Process note
    for future sweep chunks.

REGRESSIONS CAUGHT:
  None. All Python files still parse. No active code behavior
  changed (the touched Python references are user-facing strings,
  not logic paths — and the logic paths were already updated in
  Chunk 2).

NEGATIVE RESULTS:
  None. One scripting note surfaced: substring-count verification
  doesn't work when the new string contains the old. Switched
  method mid-verify and fixed the approach.

KEY INSIGHT:
  Documentation path drift is the trailing edge of any structural
  refactor. Code-path drift is caught by imports and tests; doc
  drift is invisible until someone reads the docs. The pattern
  established in Chunk 2 (move the code, update cross-file paths)
  can land cleanly without this chunk, but then readers of docs
  see stale information. Chunk 5 closes that gap.

  A reusable lesson: for any multi-file refactor, schedule a
  documentation-sweep chunk as a follow-up even when the code
  already works. The cost is small; the benefit is zero cognitive
  friction for the next person reading the docs. This is a
  hygiene pattern, not a governance rule — but worth codifying
  as a default cleanup step for future refactors.

CHRONICLE END (Session 21 Addendum 5 — documentation path sweep)

SESSION: 2026-04-21 (Session 22 Addendum 1 — BUILD.py bug fix + exhaustive re-sweep)
VERSIONS: Acervator 3.13.7 (unchanged) / SADP 1.26 → 1.27
TITLE: The Chunk 2 Audit Hole — Exhaustive Beats Scoped
================================================================================

First Session 22 work. Operator reported a real bug: BUILD.py crashing
with 'Unable to find data\\historical' when trying to bundle the app
via PyInstaller. Root-cause analysis found three issues, fixed all
three, and surfaced a valuable process lesson.

WHAT WAS BUILT:

  - Acervator_win.spec and Acervator_mac.spec gained two helper
    functions: _build_graceful_datas(project_root) filters the
    datas list for paths that actually exist, skipping missing
    optional paths with a printed warning; _read_acervator_
    version(project_root) reads __version__ from src/__init__.py
    so FileDescription tracks the current release dynamically.

  - Spec datas list now probes sadp/RAIntSimBat/ first with the
    legacy RAIntSimBat/ as a fallback. This means a frozen
    bundle built from Session 21+ works correctly AND a bundle
    built from a pre-Session-21 zip still works. Graceful
    forward + backward compatibility.

  - 10 additional live files with bare RAIntSimBat/ path
    references updated: execution_discipline.py docstring,
    ADR-003 body, SRS 3 refs, SPEC-CORE and SPEC 2 each,
    ARTIFACTS.json MASTER_SUMMARY + regen_command, NEXT_
    SESSION_ORDERS Battery MASTER line, install.sh exclude
    rule, RULE_REGISTRY 3 live rule text refs (line 882
    historical R54 reason field preserved).

KEY DECISIONS AND RATIONALE:

  - Why graceful-datas vs required-datas. data/historical is
    populated by download_archive.py which takes 15 minutes and
    needs network. For a fresh build on a machine without
    network access, that's a blocker. But the app degrades
    gracefully at runtime — it has ASSET_PERIODS anchors
    embedded and a runtime cache system. Making the build
    inherit that graceful behavior (warn but don't fail) aligns
    the build contract with the runtime contract.

  - Why keep legacy fallback RAIntSimBat/ path in spec. Older
    zips (pre-Session-21) still have RAIntSimBat/ at root.
    Keeping both probes means a user can build from ANY
    version's zip without breaking. Costs nothing (failed
    probes print a single warning).

  - Why dynamic FileDescription. The literal 'Acervator v3.7.0'
    had been stale for who-knows-how-many versions. Every
    release bump would require a manual edit to the spec
    files — easy to forget. Reading __version__ from src/
    eliminates the drift class entirely.

  - Why SADP 1.26 to 1.27. Graceful-datas and dynamic-version
    are real build capabilities that weren't there before.
    SADP version history shows capability changes bumped; pure
    cleanup didn't. This is capability.

  - Why R28 FL inversion for optional inputs. R28 says fail
    LOUDLY when a required resource is missing. data/historical
    is optional at build time (app runs fine without it). So
    the correct failure mode is NOT R28-style (hard error);
    it's R28-inverted (warn but continue). R28 remains correct
    for required runtime inputs.

REGRESSIONS CAUGHT:
  None — the fix addresses an existing bug without introducing
  new issues. Both specs parse cleanly via ast.parse. All JSON
  files remain valid. The 13 path updates all hit target
  strings on first attempt (benefit of precise pre-inspection
  grep).

NEGATIVE RESULTS:
  Session 21 Chunk 2's original audit missed 10 live files
  with bare path references. Root cause: grep was scoped to
  --include=*.py --include=*.md --include=*.json which
  excluded .spec, .sh, nested docs directories, and sadp/
  SPEC*.md. Chunk 6's documentation sweep partially closed
  this but didn't systematically cover all file types either.
  The fix (unrestricted grep) found everything in one pass.

KEY INSIGHT:

  The Chunk 2 / Chunk 6 grep pattern felt comprehensive while
  being incomplete. Three extensions covered the 'usual
  suspects' but missed .spec, .sh, and nested doc dirs. The
  lesson: 'find all references' requires either (a) grep with
  no extension filter at all, or (b) an explicit enumeration
  of every extension present in the project.

  Option (a) is simpler but can be noisy in projects with
  binary files or vendored dependencies. Option (b) is more
  work but gives scope control. For structural refactors in
  this project going forward: use option (a) with explicit
  excludes (__pycache__, .git, .zip, vendor/) rather than
  explicit includes.

  A broader lesson: audits of 'what files reference X' should
  be treated as adversarial — ask 'how could this be
  incomplete?' not just 'does this answer my question?' The
  operator's 'run Chunk 2's path sweep again' framing
  implicitly raised this question, and the answer was yes,
  10 files were missed. Useful prompting pattern for future
  audit work: challenge the sweep before trusting it.

CHRONICLE END (Session 22 Addendum 1 — BUILD.py fix + exhaustive re-sweep)
