SESSION: 2026-04-21 (Session 22 Addendum 2 — MEM-171 profit-protection fold rule)
VERSIONS: Acervator 3.13.7 (unchanged) / SADP 1.27 → 1.28
TITLE: Initial-Purchase-Price-Floor — First Patent-Flagged Feature of Session 22
================================================================================

Second Session 22 cascade. Substantial engine work. Novel IP landed.
Operator's framing 'this one may be complex' proved accurate — the
chunk ran larger than typical (~15 tool calls) but produced a
coherent end-to-end feature.

WHAT WAS BUILT:

  - Initial-Purchase-Price-Floor rule on fold rebuys. Every unit of
    target currency re-acquired through a fold must be bought back
    at a price less than or equal to its original purchase price.
    This is a strict profit-protection discipline: no unit ever
    re-enters the main position at a worse cost than where it
    started.

  - main_lots queue: per-lot provenance tracking alongside the
    existing holdings scalar. Each lot {units, initial_buy_price}.
    Invariant: sum of lot units equals holdings. Seeded at candle 0
    with the initial target/ref position.

  - 14 holdings-mutation sites instrumented: every += / -= / direct
    assignment paired with a main_lots update. Multiple passes
    needed to find them all — first mechanical scan missed 5 sites
    including the initial-seed direct assignment.

  - Fold-out: HIGHEST-PRICE-FIRST consumption of main_lots (operator
    directive). Expensive lots rotate through folds; cheap core
    stays protected. Each consumed lot becomes its own fold tranche
    with preserved initial_buy_price.

  - Fold-back: eligibility filter on initial_buy_price >= current
    rebuy price. Partial execution permitted (operator directive).
    Re-acquired units return to main_lots PRESERVING their
    initial_buy_price — compounding protection across arbitrary
    numbers of fold cycles.

  - Normal Fold legacy path: gated with 'not fold_tranches' to
    prevent aggregate-wipe of ineligible tranches.

  - tests/test_mem171_profit_protection.py: 4 invariants, all pass.
    Uses gen_from_anchors for deterministic synthetic candles.

  - ADR-004: 180-line architecture decision record. Patent-flagged.
    Captures algorithm, rejected alternatives (FIFO/LIFO/weighted-
    avg/band-aid), consequences, sources per R63.

  - MEM-171 with patent_flag=True — first patent-flagged MEM since
    the flag was added.

KEY DECISIONS AND RATIONALE:

  - Why HIGHEST-PRICE-FIRST for fold-out. Operator's explicit
    directive. Preserves the cheap core position. Alternative
    (FIFO) would rotate oldest lots regardless of price, losing
    the wealth-preservation intent. Alternative (LIFO) would
    protect the most-expensive recent purchases, the opposite
    of what we want.

  - Why preserve init_price on fold-back return, not overwrite
    with current rebuy price. Compounding protection. A unit
    bought at $60K, folded at $80K, rebought at $55K should
    still enforce the $60K floor on the NEXT fold cycle, not
    the $55K rebuy price. The unit's identity is its original
    cost basis.

  - Why additive schema (keep 'ref' field, add 'initial_buy_
    price'). Safer migration. Existing code paths that read
    t['ref'] continue to work. Only new code reads t['initial_
    buy_price']. Zero regressions in untouched paths.

  - Why RAIntSimBat-only, not mirror in simulator.py. simulator's
    fold architecture is different-shaped (_apply_profit_folding
    vs inline). R42 parity tests cover shared behaviors (FVG,
    R55 VH, R57 EPM), not fold-accounting internals, so parity
    remains green. Porting is a separate design decision.

  - Why SADP 1.27 to 1.28. Novel engine capability with IP
    value. The three-phase governance pattern considered
    (ship non-blocking, reconcile, promote) does not apply here
    because this is a NEW feature, not a constraint on existing
    behavior. Direct bump.

REGRESSIONS CAUGHT:

  The first invariant test run failed: main_lots summed to 0.0003
  BTC less than holdings after a synthetic 2000-candle sim. Root
  cause: my mechanical scan for instrumented sites looked only
  for 'holdings +=' and 'holdings -=', missing:

    (a) line 1011 'holdings = target / ref' — the initial-seed
        direct assignment at run_v3192 startup,
    (b) line 2100 Inferno deploy buy,
    (c) line 2145 shadow-position sell,
    (d) line 2178 shadow deposit buy,
    (e) line 2203 auxiliary shad-add buy.

  After adding instrumentation at all 5 sites, invariant_ok=True
  and all 4 tests green.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:

  None regarding the feature. One process cost: the chunk exceeded
  typical complexity budget. R64 ceilings of ~10-12 tool calls per
  chunk are designed for single atomic deliverables; this chunk
  ran ~15 because the deliverable was a novel engine feature with
  debug iteration baked in. Operator's 'may be complex' framing
  at chunk-start implicitly sanctioned the larger scope.

KEY INSIGHT — technical:

  Per-unit cost-basis preservation through fold cycles creates
  compounding discipline. Each rotation strengthens the
  protection rather than resetting it. The naive mental model
  is 'sell high, rebuy lower' (positive per-cycle arithmetic).
  The strong model is 'every unit locks in a gain vs its
  original purchase' — a tighter constraint that produces
  better long-run outcomes even if it reduces per-cycle fold
  activity. BTC 2023 smoke improved $31,651 → $32,913 advantage
  under the new rule, about 4% better, consistent with 'prevents
  bad rebuys' theory.

KEY INSIGHT — process:

  Grepping for instrumentation sites must cover not just
  mutation operators (+=, -=) but ALSO plain = direct
  assignments. The line-1011 initial-seed site was invisible
  to my first scan because 'holdings =' (no +/-) is easy to
  filter out when looking for mutations. But from the
  standpoint of 'every change to holdings needs lot tracking,'
  a direct assignment at initialization IS a change (from
  0 to target/ref). Future refactors of similar invariant-
  tracking shape should scan three patterns: +=, -=, and
  plain =. Added to the lessons-for-future-audits list.

CHRONICLE END (Session 22 Addendum 2 — MEM-171 profit-protection fold)

SESSION: 2026-04-21 (Session 22 Addendum 3 — MEM-172 drift debug + patch)
VERSIONS: Acervator 3.13.7 (unchanged) / SADP 1.28 → 1.29
TITLE: The Shadow Leak — Multi-Tracker Position Accounting Under HIFO
================================================================================

Third Session 22 cascade. Debugging chunk following the Addendum 2
measurement that surfaced 20/39 invariant failures. Added debug
instrumentation, traced the leak to shadow and REH liquidations
overshooting main_lots, applied identical cap fix to both, verified
39/39 invariants now hold.

WHAT WAS BUILT:

  - DEBUG_MEM171 env-var-gated drift detector in the candle loop.
    Logs first drift transition with cumulative trade counter
    deltas. Negligible cost when disabled. Retained for future
    debug use.

  - Cap at both shadow liquidation (line 2140) and REH dump
    (line 2044). Pattern: compute _effective = min(declared_qty,
    main_lots_sum, holdings). Sell only what's actually there,
    with proportional fee/profit adjustment. Reset subsystem
    state unchanged.

  - SADP 1.28 -> 1.29 version bump. Engine correctness is a
    SADP-governance concern — drift-free lot accounting is a
    real capability improvement, not cleanup.

KEY DECISIONS AND RATIONALE:

  - Why cap rather than redesign. Two options for fixing the
    overlap: (a) prevent fold-out from consuming shadow/REH-
    marked units (preserves declared quantities), (b) cap
    liquidations at actual inventory (accepts that fold-out may
    have taken some shadow/REH units). Option (a) requires
    marking lots as shadow/REH and excluding them from HIFO
    selection — complex, changes fold-out behavior. Option (b)
    is mechanical, surgical, preserves existing fold-out
    semantics. Chose (b). The semantic correctness of (a) vs
    (b) is debatable: is "shadow" a pledge or a marker? The
    engine treats it as a marker that can be overwritten by
    subsequent fold activity. (b) aligns with that stance.

  - Why reset declared_qty (shad_qty, reh_qty) to 0 even when
    only partial liquidation fired. The shadow/REH subsystem
    state is conceptually "cleared" when its trigger fires,
    regardless of actual inventory. Keeping shad_qty > 0 after
    a partial liquidation would create zombie state in the
    subsystem. Cleaner to fully clear.

  - Why proportional fee/profit adjustment. If shad_qty = 1.0
    but _effective = 0.3, we're selling 30% of what shadow
    declared. The _s_profit calculation uses shad_usd_spent
    (total USD originally committed to shadow). Using the full
    shad_usd_spent against a partial sale would over-count the
    cost basis. Multiplying by _effective/shad_qty ratio
    produces a coherent per-unit profit measurement.

  - Why SADP 1.28 -> 1.29 (capability bump, not patch bump).
    Drift-free lot tracking at engine scale enables CHK-017
    (test promotion), simulator port, and any future work
    that builds on lot accounting. That's expanded capability,
    not just bug fix.

REGRESSIONS CAUGHT:

  None. R42 parity 4/4 held throughout debugging and patching.
  MEM-171 synthetic test 4/4 held. Single-sim invariant test
  passed pre-fix (it doesn't exercise the shadow/REH paths as
  heavily as real candle data); post-fix it still passes.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:

  One false start: applied shadow cap alone, expected 20/39 ->
  small failures. Got 20/39 -> 19/39 — only 1 sim fixed. REH
  had the same bug, needed the same fix. Lesson: when debugging
  multi-site consistency bugs, fix ALL sites matching the
  pattern, not just the first one identified. Trace evidence
  (sh=286, reh=2+) in the debug log showed both subsystems
  active at drift candles, but I didn't read the reh counter
  carefully on the first pass.

KEY INSIGHT — technical:

  Multi-tracker position accounting has a fundamental tension
  with content-aware consumption policies. If the primary
  position queue is consumed by a policy (HIGHEST-PRICE-FIRST,
  LIFO, FIFO, etc.) and secondary trackers hold pointers to
  specific subsets, the policy can eat into those subsets
  silently. The subsystem later tries to operate on its
  declared pointer scope and finds it empty or partial.

  The pattern generalizes beyond accumulation engines. Any
  system with multiple position layers (tax lots, hedge
  overlays, regulatory reserves, etc.) sharing a common
  underlying inventory needs either:
  (a) mutual awareness (layers exclude each other's marked
      units from consumption), or
  (b) defensive reconciliation at liquidation time (cap
      sells at actual available inventory).

  (b) is simpler but less semantically pure. (a) is cleaner
  but requires coupling between layers that complicates the
  architecture. Choice depends on how "permanent" each
  layer's claim is meant to be.

KEY INSIGHT — advantage jump:

  $3.76M -> $17.19M -> $51.85M as drift was progressively
  eliminated. This is not the FEATURE producing more profit;
  it's the ENGINE having correct state. The fold/scrum/target-
  growth math uses (holdings - shad_qty) expressions that
  were corrupted by negative holdings. Fixing the drift
  enabled the engine to make accurate decisions about how
  aggressively to accumulate. The headline number is
  spectacular but the real lesson is: bugs that don't crash
  can silently erode correctness for a long time. Invariants
  that check coherence between state representations are the
  only way to catch them.

CHRONICLE END (Session 22 Addendum 3 — drift debug + patch)

SESSION: 2026-04-21 (Session 22 Addendum 4 — 78-sim extended battery acceptance)
VERSIONS: Acervator 3.13.7 (unchanged) / SADP 1.29 (unchanged)
TITLE: Governance of Measurement — Envelope Acceptance as Design Invariant
================================================================================

Fourth Session 22 cascade. Not a new feature, not a bug fix — an
ACCEPTANCE chunk. The 78-sim extended battery measured the behavior
of MEM-171 under stress. Operator reviewed the numbers and formally
accepted them. This turns a set of measurements into a design
invariant recorded in ADR-004.

WHAT WAS BUILT:

  - ADR-004 'Measured behavior envelope' section. Captures the
    78-sim results as the canonical characterization of MEM-171:
    71/78 wins, 78/78 invariants, $172.9M aggregate, 7 losses
    clustered in catastrophic bears (-59% to -94%), loss
    magnitudes $0.98 to $159.44. Governance statement: envelope
    changes require ADR amendment.

  - MEM-173 acceptance decision record with operator verbatim
    framing. Captures what WAS accepted, what alternatives were
    rejected (relief valve, amortization, regime-aware suspend),
    and the governance process for future changes.

KEY DECISIONS AND RATIONALE:

  - Why no SADP version bump. Session 22 Addendum 4 is
    acceptance + documentation. No new capability landed in
    SADP's enforcement surface, no new rule or invariant, no
    code change. Past pattern: documentation-only chunks don't
    bump SADP. This continues that pattern.

  - Why extend ADR-004 in place rather than create ADR-005.
    ADR-004 documents the algorithm. The measured envelope is
    a PROPERTY of that algorithm, not a new decision.
    Extending ADR-004 keeps the complete algorithm
    characterization in one place. ADR-005+ is reserved for
    future decisions that CHANGE the envelope.

  - Why preserve the tuning options as 'available but not
    taken.' They represent legitimate alternative designs the
    operator rejected for now. If business conditions change
    (e.g., the engine needs to recover better in partial-
    recovery bears), those options are pre-thought and
    retrievable without starting from scratch.

  - Why the 'governance codification' framing. An accepted
    measurement becomes structurally load-bearing in the
    system. Future refactors that affect fold mechanics
    should check whether they still produce the accepted
    envelope. If they don't, that's a design decision
    requiring operator review, not an implementation detail.

REGRESSIONS CAUGHT:

  None — this is an acceptance chunk, not a code change.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:

  None. The 78-sim run already happened in Chunk 4; this
  chunk just codifies it.

KEY INSIGHT — on measurement governance:

  Bug fixes, feature additions, and refactors are the
  expected types of code work. Measurement acceptance is a
  quieter but equally important activity: it turns empirical
  data into a design invariant. Without that codification,
  measurements drift out of institutional memory, and future
  work re-opens questions that were already answered.

  The 78-sim battery, now codified as MEM-171's behavior
  envelope, serves as a regression benchmark. If some future
  change causes 2020 COVID to drop from 13/13 wins to 10/13,
  that IS a regression — even if nothing else breaks — because
  the accepted envelope promised 13/13. The ADR-004 envelope
  section makes that check structurally possible.

  Similarly, the 7 accepted losses provide a floor: any
  future change that eliminates them (e.g., a relief valve)
  is also a change to the envelope and requires the same
  governance process. This prevents inadvertent silent
  changes to the protection contract.

KEY INSIGHT — on protection vs recovery:

  The measured data clarifies an architectural question: is
  strict cost-basis discipline a weakness or a feature?
  Operator's acceptance is definitive: it's a feature. The
  engine's loss magnitudes ($0.98 to $159) vs passive baseline
  losses ($256-$376) in the same catastrophic conditions show
  the protection working as designed. The 'trapped capital
  waiting for impossible recovery' concern is real but the
  alternative (relaxing the rule to capture partial
  recoveries) would expose capital to further downside in
  sustained bears. Strict protection with small losses beats
  loose discipline with large recoveries-that-don't-come.

CHRONICLE END (Session 22 Addendum 4 — 78-sim extended battery acceptance)

SESSION: 2026-04-21 (Session 22 Addendum 5 — CHK-017 structural enforcement)
VERSIONS: Acervator 3.13.7 (unchanged) / SADP 1.29 → 1.30
TITLE: Closing the Governance Loop on MEM-171
================================================================================

Fifth Session 22 cascade. Promotes the MEM-171 profit-protection
invariant test to a blocking CHK gate. Completes the governance
chain: ADR-004 (design) → MEM-171 (feature) → MEM-172 (drift fix) →
MEM-173 (envelope acceptance) → CHK-017 (structural enforcement).

WHAT WAS BUILT:

  - _handler_mem171_profit_protection_tests in sadp/checklist.py.
    Mirrors CHK-015 R42 pattern: imports the test file, iterates
    module-level test_ functions, runs each, collects AssertionError
    and general Exception details, returns (pass_bool, message).
    On failure, the message points the developer at
    DEBUG_MEM171=1 for candle-level drift diagnosis.

  - CHK-017 entry in sadp/CHECKLIST.json items[] array. Identical
    shape to CHK-015 with rule=MEM-171, blocks_cascade=true,
    auto_fix=null, born='Session 22 Addendum 5 (MEM-174)'.

  - SADP 1.29 -> 1.30 version bump. Past convention holds that
    new structural enforcement is a capability change even when
    no engine code moves.

KEY DECISIONS AND RATIONALE:

  - Why ship blocking from birth (streak=1) instead of the three-
    phase governance pattern Session 21 established. The pattern
    applies when a CHK is added to code that might already have
    drifted from the rule it enforces. Here the rule is MEM-171's
    invariants, and MEM-173 already validated them at 78/78 under
    stress. There is no pre-existing drift to reconcile. Shipping
    blocking immediately aligns with CHK-015's Session 21
    precedent under the same reasoning.

  - Why no auto_fix. Test failures indicate real bookkeeping
    drift in the lot accounting — the MEM-172 pattern. The fix
    requires human diagnosis (identify which site mutates
    holdings without main_lots syncing, or which secondary
    tracker overshoots). Per ORDER 5.5 invariant (auto_fix
    table = inverse of cascade), the lack of auto_fix is
    correct because no cascade step makes a drift failure
    pass. The handler's failure message even tells the
    developer where to start: DEBUG_MEM171=1.

  - Why SADP 1.29 -> 1.30 and not stay at 1.29. This is new
    structural enforcement, not documentation. CHK-017
    changes what 'ready' means in the cascade. That is a
    capability change in SADP's governance surface, same
    argument that bumped 1.27 -> 1.28 for MEM-171 and
    1.28 -> 1.29 for MEM-172.

  - Why this closes the governance chain. Five artifacts now
    anchor MEM-171: the ADR documents the algorithm, the
    parent MEM introduces it, the fix MEM patches a
    discovered drift, the acceptance MEM codifies the
    envelope, and the CHK structurally enforces the envelope.
    Each plays a distinct role. Together they make the
    feature load-bearing in the system — not just present,
    but protected.

REGRESSIONS CAUGHT:

  None. R42 parity held. CHK-015 still at streak=12, CHK-016
  at streak=11, and new CHK-017 ships at streak=1.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:

  None. Promotion landed cleanly on first attempt. The CHK-015
  template was close enough to reuse with only the handler
  name, test file path, and rationale updated.

KEY INSIGHT — on governance completeness:

  A feature is not done when the code lands. It's done when
  there is (a) a design record, (b) an implementation, (c)
  empirical validation, (d) accepted behavior envelope, and
  (e) structural enforcement of that envelope. Each layer
  protects the feature against a different failure mode:

    - Design record protects against 'why did we do this?'
    - Implementation protects against 'does it work?'
    - Empirical validation protects against 'does it work
      at scale and under stress?'
    - Envelope acceptance protects against 'did we agree on
      what good looks like?'
    - Structural enforcement protects against 'did we
      accidentally break it later?'

  MEM-171 took six chunks of Session 22 to build this full
  stack. The operator's per-chunk decisions (approve design,
  pick lot order, accept partial rebuy, debug the drift,
  accept the envelope, promote to gate) were each the right
  call at each stage. Collectively they produced a feature
  that is protected against six different classes of
  regression.

  The template for future patent-flagged features is now
  visible: ADR at commit time, parent MEM, debug-and-fix MEM
  if instrumentation surfaces drift, battery measurement,
  envelope acceptance MEM, CHK promotion. Six-chunk arc.

CHRONICLE END (Session 22 Addendum 5 — CHK-017 structural enforcement)

SESSION 22 POST-CLOSE ADDENDUM (2026-04-21, 14:30 UTC)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CLOSE ZIP BUILD LESSON: walk-and-exclude, not allowlist
================================================================================

On first attempt to build the Session 22 close zip, I hand-curated
an include list of ~48 specific files I knew had changed during the
session. The resulting zip was 0.95 MB with 48 files.

The correct reference (Session 21 close zip) was 2.5 MB with 301
files across 54 top-level entries, including the full src/ tree
(113 files of application code), all of docs/ (33 files), tests/
(19 files), os/ (17 files), root-level Python scripts (main.py,
render.py, etc.), PDF product manual, build scripts, specs.

Operator immediately identified the problem: 'That one is built
wrong....'

Root cause of the error: cognitive bias toward 'what changed this
session' rather than 'what does a complete project snapshot look
like.' A close zip is not a delta; it is a self-contained snapshot.

Fix: rebuild with os.walk rooted at /home/claude/work, excluding
only caches (__pycache__, .pyc, .DS_Store, .git, node_modules,
.venv, .mypy_cache, .pytest_cache) and files >20MB. Result: 285
files, 8.15 MB uncompressed / 2.63 MB compressed. Matches
Session 21's shape at 54 top-level entries. Variance in individual
file counts (docs 29 vs 33, os 11 vs 17, src 104 vs 113) is
expected natural churn over one session.

LESSON CAPTURED FOR FUTURE CLOSES:

  The close-zip build algorithm is:

      walk the work root
      exclude caches and massive binaries
      include everything else

  NOT:

      enumerate the files I remember changing

  The first approach is stateless and self-correcting. The second
  requires perfect memory of every file the session touched AND
  every file that was relevant in prior sessions. Operator
  correctly rejected the second approach; this lesson must prevent
  Session 23+ from repeating the mistake.

  Next close-zip task should use the walk-and-exclude pattern
  directly, no allowlist consideration.

Each ADR uses a compact retroactive-authorship template (~50-70
lines) with consistent structure:

    invention landed Session N)
  - Patent flag: YES header metadata
  - Context with excerpt from the MEM's summary
  - Decision to formalize as documented patent-flagged invention
  - Rationale (IP governance hygiene — JSON tag vs ADR record)
  - Full Patent flag section naming claim + related MEMs
  - Alternatives considered (with reasons for rejection)

    implementation-time context, no priority-date anchoring)

KEY DECISIONS:

  - Why compact template, not 180-line ADR-004 format. The
    invention content is already captured in the MEM entries.
    Retroactive ADRs are primarily IP-governance records, not
    new design documents. Compact format (~50-70 lines)
    preserves the essential structure (Patent flag declaration,
    Sources, Alternatives) without over-inflating.

  - Why per-MEM ADRs vs per-cluster ADRs. Preserves IP-record
    granularity. Each invention has its own prior-art-
    distinguishing claim. ADR-011 (hunger + satiety paired dual
    index) shows when pairing is appropriate; retroactive ADRs
    chose per-MEM to match the MEM granularity.

  - Why author at 2026-04-21 for Session 1-17 inventions. Best
    to author formal records sooner rather than later;
    delaying further only worsens record quality. The invention
    date is preserved in the MEM itself and in the ADR's Status
    line ('retroactive authorship 2026-04-21 for invention
    originally landed Session N').

KEY INSIGHT — DETERMINISTIC RETROACTIVE DOCUMENTATION:

  When the source material (MEM entries with rich summaries)
  already contains the substantive content, retroactive formal
  document authorship is primarily a templating exercise. The
  creative work happened at invention time; the retroactive
  work is structural hygiene. A template + data mapping +
  generation script does the job cleanly in a single tool
  call.

  This contrasts with authoring an ADR AT invention time,
  which requires live decision-making about what the decision
  IS. For retroactive authorship, the decision is already made
  and the ADR records it.

P1.8 FIXED — NUCLEAR MODE ROTATION NOTIFICATION
================================================================================

Operator directive: 'Fix P1.8 now — diagnose + patch the Nuclear
Mode single-bot-overwrite.'

DIAGNOSIS in 3 tool calls:

  1. Read nuclear_live.py _rotate_feeds (line 1153) — found that
     rotation mutates feed.asset/candles/period/symbol IN PLACE
     on the existing feed object while preserving feed.bot_id.

  2. Read bot_register_cb call sites across nuclear_live.py —
     only fires on initial spawn (line 1596) and MR-gated
     scale-up spawn (line 1769). No rotation notification.

  3. Read bot_visualizer.register_sim_run (line 1120) — keyed
     by sim_id in _live_sim_rows dict, starts with
     _remove_live_sim(sim_id) before recreating row. This means
     re-firing register on the same sim_id cleanly refreshes
     the row.

ROOT CAUSE:

  Rotation is a substantive state change (asset/period/candles
  all replaced) but is SILENT from the GUI's perspective. The
  chart area shows the new asset without the bot row or status
  reflecting why. User perceives this as overwrite of a single
  bot slot rather than as an intentional rotation in a swarm
  cycling through battery periods.

PATCH:

  ~20 lines added at end of per-feed rotation block in
  _rotate_feeds. Fires bot_register_cb with feed.bot_id and
  cfg including 'rotated': True flag. register_sim_run's
  existing remove-and-recreate behavior means the UI
  refreshes cleanly on the same sim_id.

KEY DECISIONS:

  - Why reuse bot_register_cb instead of adding a new
    rotation_cb. Minimum surface change: register_sim_run's
    remove-and-recreate already handles the semantics
    cleanly. Adding a new callback would require threading
    through NuclearLiveEngine init, NuclearLiveThread kwargs,
    demo_runner wiring, AND a new method on bot_visualizer.
    Four call sites touched for no additional information
    flow. Reuse is cheaper and semantically correct.

  - Why include 'rotated': True flag in the cfg dict. Forward
    compatibility. Current code doesn't use it but a future
    UI iteration could animate rotations differently from
    initial spawns, or collect rotation statistics, without
    needing another engine change.

  - Why NOT address n_feeds=1 or Mature Profits gate. Both
    are intentional design choices, not bugs. The operator's
    bug report was about OVERWRITE, not about swarm sizing.
    Fixing the silent-overwrite perception is the right-
    sized P1.8 response. Ergonomic improvements (n_feeds=3
    for immediate swarm visibility, or loosened mature-
    profits gate for faster scale-up) are separate decisions
    that need operator input.

  - Why SADP 1.30 -> 1.31. Rotation is now an OBSERVABLE
    event in the engine contract. Downstream consumers
    (demo_runner, any future integrators) can now react to
    rotations, distinguishing them from initial spawns via
    the 'rotated' flag. That's a capability extension, not a
    bug fix alone.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:

  None. Patch landed clean on first attempt. Diagnosis was
  direct — the code was well-commented enough that the
  missing rotation notification was obvious once the
  rotation boundary was inspected.

KEY INSIGHT — THE SILENT-MUTATION ANTIPATTERN:

  Objects that represent entities with observers (e.g. feed
  objects where a GUI observes the bot) should not be
  mutated in place without firing a corresponding event.
  The 'feed' object in nuclear_live.py has a subscribed GUI
  observer through bot_register_cb; mutating its
  asset/period/candles without a callback violates the
  observer contract silently.

  The fix pattern — re-fire the register callback on the
  same identity key with a 'rotated' discriminator — is
  cleaner than adding a new callback because the observer's
  remove-and-recreate handler was already correct; only the
  notification was missing.

  Applicable anywhere in the codebase where objects with
  subscribed observers are mutated through state-transition
  methods that forget to notify. Worth a rule or CHK in a
  future session if the pattern recurs.

KEY INSIGHT — FAILED-ATTEMPT ARCHAEOLOGY:

  When an operator says 'previous attempt failed,' look for code
  artifacts that suggest interrupted work: duplicate blocks,
  unreachable branches, orphaned imports, commented-out
  half-edits. The duplicate-except on Testnet was an obvious
  signature. Removing it in the same pass as completing the
  originally-intended work is the right clean-up opportunity.

  Generalizable: any time we're doing work in an area where
  prior attempts happened, a quick 'duplicate-content scan'
  (grep for repeated block patterns, unreachable code, near-
  identical except clauses) can surface the artifacts cheaply.

KEY INSIGHT — SHELVE VS DELETE:

  The remove strategy of 'replace with None assignment' rather
  than 'delete entirely' preserves the attribute identity for
  downstream hasattr/None checks. A stricter 'delete everything
  including the attribute' would require auditing every caller
  for AttributeError surfaces. Shelving is a lighter-weight
  revert surface: restoration = single revert per block.

  This is equivalent to the MEM-171 decision of using additive
  schema (keep 'ref' field, add 'initial_buy_price') vs
  breaking migration. Same principle: minimize blast radius
  of the change so revert and future work stay cheap.

  identically to a sim-created bot with the same settings.'

KEY INSIGHT — SCHEMA EXTENSION VS BREAKING MIGRATION:

  The BotConfig schema extension is an ADDITIVE change:
  
    old code reads existing fields → still works
    new code reads new fields → gets sensible defaults
    old cfg dicts restore → old fields honored, new fields
      default
    new cfg dicts restore → all fields honored
  
  No data migration. No breakage. This is the right
  schema-evolution pattern when the new fields are
  optional extensions, not replacements. If we'd needed to
  change an existing field's type or semantics, a migration
  would be required; here, purely additive = no migration.

P1.10 CHUNK 1 of 7 — MEM-069 + MEM-171 PORTED TO REAL BOT
================================================================================

Operator directive from the launch-safety review: 'Full parity port
— all 10 gates + 2 inventions + runtime parity test (5-8 chunks).'

Chunk 1 of 7 delivered. Ports the two patent-flagged inventions
(MEM-069 provenance fold queue + MEM-171 initial_buy_price floor)
from the sim engine to src/trading/scrumming_bot.py.

BEFORE THIS CHUNK:

  Real bot had ZERO references to main_lots, initial_buy_price,
  fold_tranches. Sim had 82. The biggest-risk gap in the parity
  matrix.

  Deployed on a volatile asset like RAVE, the real bot would
  rebuy units at prices ABOVE their original cost basis — the
  exact failure mode MEM-171 prevents. 78/78 sim invariant
  validations were non-predictive of real-bot live performance.

AFTER THIS CHUNK:

  _fold_tranches list replaces single _fold_queue_usd scalar.
  _main_lots list tracks per-lot initial_buy_price.
  Scrum consumes main_lots HIGHEST-PRICE-FIRST creating tranches.
  Fold filters eligible tranches by both ref gate AND IBP gate.
  DIST re-fold also creates tranches (closes compounding escape
  hatch).
  7/7 structural invariant tests pass.

KEY DECISIONS:

  - Why preserve legacy _fold_queue_usd and _fold_queue_ref_price
    scalars as derived aggregates. Migration compat — any existing
    consumer reading these still gets correct-looking values
    during the port period. They're no longer source of truth but
    they're correct. Clean-slate removal would require auditing
    every consumer in the project, which is a larger scope. Flag
    as P1.10 follow-up (after all chunks land, remove the legacy
    fields + update consumers).

  - Why structural tests rather than behavioral. ScrummingBot is
    async-exchange-coupled. Full behavioral tests (same candle
    data → identical trade sequences between sim and real)
    require an async exchange mock — that's the Chunk 7 scope.
    Structural tests today + behavioral tests Chunk 7 is the
    right layering.

  - Why use ticker.last as proxy initial_buy_price for inherited
    holdings. Conservative read — the actual prior cost basis is
    unknown from exchange balance alone. Using ticker.last as
    proxy means: prices below this are eligible for fold rebuy,
    prices above are not. Worst case: bot might hold a lot that
    was actually bought higher (so rebuys are too restrictive).
    Best case: bot might hold a lot that was actually bought
    lower (so rebuys are too permissive — but only above ticker
    at init, which is a narrow window). Net-neutral-to-
    conservative given no alternative data source.

  - Why HIGHEST-PRICE-FIRST on scrum consumption. Per MEM-171
    design: expensive lots need protection priority on fold-back
    because they have the tightest floor. If cheap lots filled
    the fold queue first, the expensive lots would be stuck with
    no floor on a subsequent sell, defeating the invention.

  - Why the DIST re-fold path also needed tranche creation. The
    compounding cycle (scrum → fold → dist → re-queue →
    re-fold → ...) would bypass the MEM-171 floor on every cycle
    after the first if DIST kept using the old single-scalar
    pattern. This was subtle — easy to miss in review.

KEY INSIGHT — PORTS NEED DATA-FLOW AUDIT, NOT JUST LOGIC PORT:

  Porting MEM-171's scrum and fold logic alone wasn't enough.
  The DIST re-fold path rebuilds the queue on every compounding
  cycle. Without porting THAT too, protection holds for cycle 1
  but breaks for cycle 2+.

  Pattern: when porting an invariant from A to B, trace every
  write site in A, not just the canonical ones. MEM-171 in the
  sim touches 82 code locations; scrum + fold are the canonical
  two, but re-fold, REH-dump, shadow liquidation all read/write
  the same state.

  This chunk covers scrum + fold + DIST re-fold for the real
  bot. REH-dump and shadow don't exist on the real bot path
  (they're sim-only accounting fictions). So the port surface
  is naturally smaller — but still 3 sites, not 2.

KEY INSIGHT — STRUCTURAL TESTS BRIDGE TO BEHAVIORAL TESTS:

  Full behavioral parity tests need infrastructure we don't
  have yet (async exchange mock producing deterministic ticker
  feeds). But structural tests can verify the port is
  architecturally correct RIGHT NOW: are the data structures
  present? are the decision gates present? does the source
  carry the right markers for future traceability?

  Both test types are valuable. Structural catches 'developer
  forgot to port the DIST path' today. Behavioral catches
  'developer ported the paths but the decision timing is
  subtly wrong on tick N=847' in Chunk 7.

  Layering: structural tests gate merges TODAY (CHK-019 when
  promoted); behavioral tests become the live CHK-020 LATER.

    event-loop coupling, matches existing api_validator.py
    pattern. 15s timeout guards against exchange hangs.

  - Why preflight is ADVISORY, not authoritative. The
    authoritative guard is CCXT's amount_to_precision /
    price_to_precision at order placement time. Preflight
    surfaces issues EARLY to save the operator a bot
    creation they'll have to redo. Don't duplicate the
    authoritative guard — keep it at one layer.

  - Why failure modes are non-blocking for diagnostic
    errors. If CCXT can't be imported or the preflight
    module itself errors, logging and continuing is better
    than blocking bot creation. The diagnostic tool is a
    HELP, not a GATE. Users who know what they're doing
    shouldn't be blocked by a tooling failure.

    start confirmation creates prompt fatigue which leads to
    reflexive Yes-clicking — defeats the purpose. One
    explicit confirmation per bot, with all config fields
    shown, balances friction against usability.

    to proceed'). Considered, decided against for now.

    confirmation is heavier friction than warranted at this
    stage. If live RAVE:USD experiences friction issues,

  references BEFORE claiming the extension is 'done'. Zero
  refs outside the dataclass definition = the field is an
  island.

  precision. These are also enforced authoritatively at order
  placement time by CCXT's own amount_to_precision and
  price_to_precision. So the preflight is redundant — except

  finish (before committing to bot creation + real-money
  authorization) rather than at first trade (possibly
  minutes or hours later).

  Pattern: diagnostic tooling layers above authoritative
  guards don't weaken the system — they just improve
  discovery time. Keep the authoritative guard; add
  diagnostic layers to fail earlier and more informatively.

P1.10 CHUNK 2 of 7 — BB MIDLINE GATE + DETECT/FIRE THRESHOLDS
================================================================================

Second chunk of the full parity port. Ports three runtime gates
from sim to the real bot: bb_midline_gate (from canonical
RAIntSimBat), detect_pct + fire_pct via SEARCH/TRACK/FIRE state
machine (from simulator.py — the canonical sim has these as
dead signature params).

BEFORE:
  Scrum fires on: delta>interval + BULLISH + !trend_hold
  Fold fires on: tranches + BEARISH + MEM-171 per-tranche gates

AFTER:
  Scrum fires on: delta>interval + BULLISH + !trend_hold
                  + scrum_ok (bb_pos > 0.50 if bb_midline_gate)
                  + target_fires (state machine = 'fire')
  Fold fires on: tranches + BEARISH + fold_ok_midline
                 + MEM-171 per-tranche gates

6 TRANSITIONS IN THE STATE MACHINE:
  SEARCH→FIRE (fast move to band, skips TRACK)
  SEARCH→TRACK (dist crossed detect threshold)
  TRACK→FIRE (within fire threshold of band)
  TRACK→SEARCH (retreat below detect × 0.5)
  FIRE→TRACK (off band, still in detect zone)
  FIRE→SEARCH (retreat below detect × 0.5)
  + implicit: FIRE→SEARCH after trade fires (reset)

KEY DECISIONS:

  - Why lift from simulator.py rather than RAIntSimBat for
    the detect/fire logic. RAIntSimBat has these as dead
    signature params — they're passed but not used in the
    function body. simulator.py is the only place where
    they actually drive decisions. If the port had
    mechanically followed RAIntSimBat, Chunk 2 would have
    been a no-op port of two unused parameters.

    Operator's 'all 10 gates' directive implicitly treats
    simulator.py as authoritative for gate semantics the
    canonical engine doesn't implement. Worth capturing
    this as a principle: when the canonical sim and the
    simulator.py tab diverge, pick the one that ACTUALLY
    runs the logic, not the one with the fullest signature.

  - Why degrade permissively when bb_result is None. The
    pre-chunk-2 behavior was: scrum fires when the 3 basic
    conditions pass, no gate check. Falling back to the same
    behavior (target_fires=True if no BB data) keeps the bot
    functional during BB computation hiccups (insufficient
    candles, exchange error fetching OHLCV, etc.) rather
    than silently refusing to trade. The alternative (fail
    closed when BB data missing) would have been safer in
    one sense but would have required hundreds of lines of
    'why isn't my bot trading?' debugging in production.

  - Why reset state machine after scrum fires. Without the
    reset, FIRE latches. Every tick where price is still
    near the band sees mode='fire' from the previous tick,
    passes the gate, and fires another scrum. Rapid-fire
    scrumming into a single price excursion destroys the
    whole point of having a state machine.

    Simulator.py had this correctly via the R44 sadp comment
    but only in the FIRE exit transitions. The post-trade
    reset is a separate line. Easy to miss in a port.

  - Why 3 different tolerances exist in the bot's BB logic.
      bb_tolerance_pct (default 1%) — Landing Strip detection
      fire_pct (default 0.5%) — FIRE state transition
      bullseye tolerance (0.5% hardcoded) — BB Bullseye Chunk 3
    They serve different purposes. Landing Strip looks for
    consolidation (Heikin-Ashi tight candles NEAR the band,
    not AT it). FIRE detects proximity for scrum firing. BB
    Bullseye detects exact-touch for rapid fire. Unifying
    them would conflate three distinct behaviors. Keep them
    separate.

KEY INSIGHT — DEAD SIGNATURE PARAMETERS:

  RAIntSimBat.run_v3192 accepts detect_pct=0.75 and
  fire_pct=0.005 in its function signature and even has
  them in the docstring. But the function body never
  references them. They're legacy cruft from an earlier
  design iteration.

  Ports that mechanically follow the function signature
  produce mechanically correct but semantically empty
  code. This is a good case for: ALWAYS read the body,
  not just the signature. Parameter docstrings are
  claims, not contracts.

  Would be nice to add a linter check: unused function
  parameters in engine functions. Low priority since
  this is caught by human review when porting, but
  worth capturing.

KEY INSIGHT — FOLD BLOCK TWO-SITE MODIFICATION:

  Adding the fold_ok_midline gate required TWO changes:
    1. Outer conditional: if self._fold_tranches and
       is_bearish and fold_ok_midline:
    2. HOLD FOLD log branches: new elif for when tranches
       exist, TA is bearish, but midline gate blocks

  If only the outer conditional had been updated, the
  gate would be SILENT — operator would see no fold
  firing and no log explaining why. That's exactly the
  opposite of 'legible behavior'.

  Pattern: when adding a gate, trace every control path
  that could be AFFECTED by it, not just the one that
  CONSUMES it. The consumer is one edit; the observability
  might be 2-4 more.

P1.10 CHUNK 3 of 7 — BB BULLSEYE + HEDGE REBALANCE
================================================================================

Third chunk of the full parity port. Ports three gates: BB Bullseye
Check (close + wick touch detection on both BB bands), Hedge
Rebalance (separate USD reserve for dip buying), Hedge Balance
(reserve size, replenished from fold profit).

KEY INSIGHTS THIS CHUNK:

  1. HEDGE BUYS MUST INTEGRATE WITH MEM-171.

     A naive hedge (just buy asset, don't touch _main_lots)
     would silently violate MEM-171 on the next scrum cycle:
     HIGHEST-PRICE-FIRST consumption wouldn't see the hedge-
     bought units. Appending to _main_lots with the current
     fill price preserves the invariant.

     Parallel problem pattern to Chunk 1's DIST re-fold catch:
     any code path that adds units to holdings must also
     append to _main_lots. If hedge had been added in
     isolation before MEM-171 existed, this would have been
     a retrofit scare. Pattern for future features that
     create assets: at merge time, grep for _main_lots.append
     to confirm the new asset path integrates.

  2. BULLSEYE IS AN OVERRIDE, NOT A REPLACEMENT.

     The state machine (Chunk 2) still runs every tick.
     Bullseye just bypasses the gate check for one tick.
     This keeps the state machine coherent — next tick, if
     price moved off band, the FIRE→TRACK or FIRE→SEARCH
     transition fires correctly.

     A naive replacement (bullseye detection sets mode=FIRE
     directly) would have broken the state machine by
     setting mode to a value the normal transition rules
     wouldn't have produced. The override pattern preserves
     monotonic state-machine evolution.

  3. HEDGE NOT GATED BY BB_MIDLINE_GATE IS DELIBERATE.

     Scrum and fold are gated by bb_midline_gate. Hedge is
     NOT. Reason: hedge is DOWNSIDE PROTECTION and must
     work in bearish regimes by design. Adding midline
     gating would narrow the hedge activation window (it
     already requires bb_pos<0.40 which is below midline
     anyway — but adding another lower-bound would make
     it fire only in ~40% of candles instead of ~50%).

     More importantly: the bb_midline_gate serves the
     LONG-TERM accumulation rhythm (scrum above, fold
     below). Hedge serves short-term drawdown protection.
     Different timescales, different gates.

  4. HEDGE REPLENISHMENT CAP USES INITIAL, NOT TARGET.

     Profit-folding grows target_balance over time. If the
     hedge cap scaled with target, the reserve could grow
     indefinitely as profits compound. Bounding at the
     initial operator-specified amount preserves capital
     allocation intent. Operator decided '$200 for hedge'
     — that decision shouldn't be overridden by the engine.

  5. ORDERING OF THE HEDGE BLOCK MATTERS.

     Placed AFTER fold (which uses delta to compute rebuys)
     and BEFORE distribute (which handles post-rebuy excess).
     This ordering ensures:
       - Hedge triggers on post-fold delta (not pre-fold)
       - Hedge buys don't double-count with dist sells
       - Profit folding target adjustment runs first so
         hedge uses updated target_balance for gap check

     Order was determined by reading the canonical sim's
     block sequence and mirroring.

P1.10 CHUNK 4 of 7 — BAND TRAVEL + READ RATE
================================================================================

Fourth chunk. Ports Band Travel (secondary harvest trigger) and
Read Rate (tick-skip throttle for expensive exchange+TA calls).

KEY INSIGHTS:

  1. BASELINE FRESHNESS ACROSS ALL TRADE PATHS.

     Band Travel's _last_trade_price is the reference for
     computing the 'how far has price moved since last
     trade' metric. If only scrum updates it, then a chain
     of folds and hedges and dists would leave the baseline
     anchored at the ancient scrum price. After many such
     trades, even a small move would register as a huge
     'band travel' and trigger phantom scrums.

     Fix: update at ALL FOUR trade paths (scrum, fold,
     hedge, dist). This is parallel to Chunk 3's MEM-171
     integration lesson — any code path that affects trade
     position must also touch related invariants.

     General pattern: features with per-trade state need
     the state-update audit at merge time. Trivial to miss;
     silent failure mode; hard to catch in review without
     the explicit checklist.

  2. READ RATE GATING LEVEL MATTERS.

     Option A: gate at scheduler — scheduler decides
     whether to call tick() at all. Problem: coordinator
     and phantom and indicator update logic live inside
     the scheduler call; gating there would stop all of
     them. Wrong granularity.

     Option B (chosen): gate at TOP of tick(). Counter
     increments every call. On non-action ticks, return
     early AFTER checking _initialised. Init tick always
     runs — otherwise a fresh bot would skip for 5 minutes
     before connecting. Expensive path (get_ohlcv +
     compute_all + detect_bb_proximity) is what we actually
     want to throttle.

     The init-skip interaction is easy to miss in a direct
     port because the sim doesn't have the same async-
     exchange-setup gymnastics. Watching for it required
     knowing the real bot's lifecycle.

  3. WHY RESTORE-ON-SEARCH IS AUTOMATIC HERE.

     Simulator.py caches the SEARCH-mode skip value and
     explicitly restores it when transitioning back from
     TRACK/FIRE to SEARCH. That's because simulator.py
     has a sim-tick loop that reuses the cached value.

     In scrumming_bot.py's async model, the skip is
     recomputed from scratch every tick based on current
     _scrum_target_mode. So the 'restore' happens
     automatically — no explicit caching needed. Simpler
     and equally correct.

     General principle: when porting state-machine logic
     across fundamentally different execution models
     (sim loop vs. async), the port should follow the
     target model's idioms, not mechanically mirror the
     source's caching strategies.

  4. TREND-HOLD OVERRIDE LOG IS OBSERVABILITY, NOT LOGIC.

     Adding the TREND-HOLD OVERRIDE log seems cosmetic,
     but without it the operator has no way to tell
     whether:
       (a) trend_hold suppressed a scrum (existing case)
       (b) trend_hold fired but was overridden by BT
       (c) trend_hold didn't fire at all

     All three produce similar bot.log output otherwise.
     The override log is the only way operators
     distinguish (b) from (c) in live traces.

     Parallel to the HOLD FOLD log branches added in
     Chunk 2 (midline-blocked vs. TA-blocked vs. tranche-
     gated). Legibility of gate behavior is a first-class
     concern, not an afterthought.

P1.10 CHUNK 5 of 7 — PHANTOM REGIME (MULTI-TF SUPPRESSION)
================================================================================

Fifth chunk. This one is a BUG FIX masquerading as a feature port.

The pre-Chunk-5 behavior early-returned the tick on any higher-TF
lock, blocking ALL trades including folds, hedge buys, and DIST.
That directly contradicts the canonical sim's asymmetric semantics:
phantom locks suppress HARVEST only; downside protection is never
blocked. This was a silent-correctness violation — the kind that
passes invariant tests and shows up only in live divergence.

FAILURE MODE CLOSED:

  Operator bot running during a volatile event. 4h phantom
  detects overbought, registers a bullish lock. Main bot has
  $500 of fold tranches ready for dip-buying. Price drops 8%.
  Under pre-chunk-5 behavior: every tick's phantom-locked
  check returns early, fold rebuys skipped entirely. Bot
  sits on unspent capital through the dip, then phantom lock
  expires, then... fold tranches eventually rebuy but at
  post-dip prices, much less favorable than if they'd fired
  during the dip.

  Under Chunk 5 (canonical sim semantics): phantom lock is
  noted, scrum is suppressed, but fold eligibility check
  still runs. Fold rebuys fire during the dip. Capital is
  deployed. The original purpose of 'having tranches queued'
  is achieved.

  Silent failure mode. No error log. No invariant violation.
  Just 'bot isn't buying even though price is way below my
  tranches' — confusing, frustrating, and costly.

KEY INSIGHTS:

  1. PRE-PORT DIVERGENCE CAN BE SILENT-INCORRECT.

     MEM-181's diagnostic said 'real bot is substantially
     divergent from sim'. Chunks 1-4 fixed structural and
     semantic gaps that were VISIBLE in code inspection —
     missing fields, missing decision sites, missing state
     machines. Chunk 5 is different: the gate CHECK was
     there, it just applied the result to the wrong SCOPE.

     Visible-missing things are the easy fixes. Inverted
     semantics are the hard ones — they pass every local
     test because locally the code does something
     reasonable. Only a behavioral parity harness that
     compares aggregate outcomes (sim vs. real on shared
     candle data) catches the class.

     CHUNK 7 HAS JUST GROWN IN IMPORTANCE. What looked like
     a 'nice validation' is now 'the only way to prove
     the port is actually correct'.

  2. OCCURRENCE-BOUND TESTS AS DOWNSIDE-LEAK GUARDS.

     Most presence tests use 'count >= N' — verify the
     feature is there at least N times. Chunk 5's
     scrum-gate test uses BOUNDED count: '3 <= count <= 15'.

     If too FEW references: the lock flag is inert,
     nothing gates on it, feature is silently disabled.

     If too MANY references: the lock flag is probably
     leaking into fold/hedge/dist paths, violating the
     downside-protection invariant.

     Permissive bounds accommodate legit usage (state
     init + 2 scrum_ok assignments + conditional logging +
     diagnostic uses = ~4-8 refs). Upper bound catches
     gross accidental reuse.

     Pattern: when a feature has an EXCLUSION domain (this
     must NOT appear in these paths), bounded occurrence
     tests are a lightweight guard against accidental
     overreach. Cheaper than full control-flow analysis;
     good enough for common mistakes.

  3. INFRASTRUCTURE WAS ALREADY CORRECT — CONSUMPTION
     WAS WRONG.

     The phantom balance + TradeLock + TimeframeCoordinator
     infrastructure was already present in scrumming_bot.py
     from v1.1 (pre-port era). Phantom bots were registering
     locks correctly. Coordinator.is_locked() worked.

     What was wrong: the MAIN BOT's consumption of the
     lock flag. Early-return pattern instead of scrum-only
     conjunct. The port didn't need to build new
     infrastructure, just re-wire the consumer.

     Pattern: when diagnosing cross-module bugs, check
     CONSUMER side even if PRODUCER side looks correct.
     Infrastructure-producer-consumer splits hide bugs on
     the consumer side because the producer is usually
     the more complex code and gets reviewed more.

  4. LEGACY EARLY-RETURN IS A COMMON ANTIPATTERN.

     'if bad_condition: log+return' feels defensive and
     safe. But when 'bad_condition' is actually a
     'suppression applies only to subset of paths' signal,
     the early-return over-applies it. 'Log and continue,
     set a flag, let downstream checks decide' is the
     correct idiom for asymmetric gates.

     Any time a port or review sees 'return' inside a
     lock/check block, worth asking: is this truly blocking
     EVERY downstream operation, or is the block scoped to
     only some?

P1.10 CHUNK 6 of 7 — SLIP FN / ACTUAL FILL CAPTURE
================================================================================

Sixth chunk. Semantically different from Chunks 1-5 — the sim
models slippage; the real bot doesn't need to model it because
the actual exchange reports actual fills. What was missing was
the downstream CONSUMPTION of those fills.

PRE-CHUNK-6 STATE:

  _execute_sell/buy placed the order via guarded_place_order,
  got back an Order response, and threw it away. Every caller
  used ticker.last (the intended price at tick start) for all
  downstream state.

  Under even modest slippage (0.1-0.5%) common on Coinbase
  during high-volume periods, this caused silent divergence:
    - MEM-171 tranche refs = intended sell price, so fold gate
      'price < tranche.ref' was looser than actual sell
      position justified
    - Hedge lot basis = intended price, so subsequent scrums
      floored too generously
    - DIST re-fold tranche refs = intended price, so DIST
      re-fold cycle bypassed the MEM-171 floor
    - Zero-balance entry seed = intended price, polluting the
      FOUNDATIONAL cost basis for the bot's entire lifetime

  Silent because: R55 Verify Hit already protects PRE-trade
  (cancels orders whose projected slippage breaches per-asset-
  class tolerance). R55 solves 'don't place bad orders'.
  Chunk 6 solves 'record what the exchange actually did'.

CHUNK 6 IMPLEMENTATION:

  _execute_sell and _execute_buy now return Optional[float]:
  the actual fill price. Extraction chain: Order.average →
  Order.price → fallback to intended argument.

  5 caller sites rewired to capture the return:
    scrum → sell_fill
    fold → buy_fill
    hedge → hedge_fill
    DIST → dist_fill
    zero-balance entry → entry_fill

  Each fill variable feeds downstream state that previously
  used ticker.last:
    - tranche refs
    - _main_lots initial_buy_price (cost basis)
    - _last_trade_price (band-travel baseline)
    - volume stats
    - trade.filled emit price
    - log messages now include 'intended $X, slip +0.xyz%'

KEY INSIGHTS:

  1. PORTING ACROSS EXECUTION MODELS REQUIRES SEMANTIC
     TRANSLATION NOT LITERAL TRANSLATION.

     Sim's slip_pct_fn is an INPUT: user provides slippage
     model as a function. Sim calls _fill_price(p, side)
     internally and that output feeds tranche refs, lot
     basis, baselines.

     Real bot's 'slip model' is the ACTUAL EXCHANGE. The
     port isn't 'add a slip_pct_fn parameter to scrumming
     bot' — that would be mechanical and wrong. The port
     is 'capture what the exchange returns and use it the
     same way sim uses _fill_price's output'. Same
     downstream data flow; completely different source.

     Parallel to Chunk 2's dead-signature-params insight:
     read the function BODY to understand what the
     parameter DOES, not just the signature claim.

  2. DEFAULT RETURN VALUE TELLS A STORY.

     Pre-Chunk-6, _execute_sell returned None. That's
     itself a code smell: 'no caller cared about the
     trade outcome'. When a function does substantive
     I/O (places a real order, waits for a real response)
     and returns None, the question 'what about the
     response?' is unanswered.

     Pattern: when porting, flag every function whose
     sim-side equivalent produces computed state. Check
     that the real-bot equivalent captures and propagates
     that state. Discarded return values are often bugs
     waiting to be found.

  3. SLIPPAGE VISIBILITY IS FIRST-CLASS UX.

     Adding 'intended $X.XX, slip +0.xyz%' to every
     FILLED log gives operators direct visibility into
     exchange fill quality. Without this, operators can
     only see that P&L is drifting — not WHY. A Coinbase
     connector that consistently fills 0.3% worse than
     expected would compound silently into major P&L drift
     over weeks of operation.

     Observability of slip is as important as correctness
     of slip accounting. One enables the other to be
     validated in production.

  4. TEST DEBT FROM CHUNK EVOLUTION — CAUGHT AND FIXED.

     Chunk 4's Test P asserted literal string pattern
     'self._last_trade_price = ticker.last'. Chunk 6
     changed every one of those assignments to use
     actual-fill variables.

     Running the full 26-test suite caught this
     immediately. Good signal. Fix pattern:

       Old test: relaxed to broader invariant (regex match
         any RHS assigned to _last_trade_price — 4+ sites)
       New test (Chunk 6 Z): stricter invariant (must use
         named fill variables sell_fill/buy_fill/
         hedge_fill/dist_fill)

     Cumulative coverage grows. Each test has clear
     semantic ownership: Chunk 4 P owns 'baseline is
     updated at all trade sites'; Chunk 6 Z owns 'those
     updates use actual fills'.

     Opposite of test-replacement: test-refinement. When
     a later chunk makes an earlier invariant more
     specific, keep the earlier test at its original
     generality and add a new test for the specific
     strengthening. The two together describe the full
     invariant history.

  5. CCXT ORDER DATACLASS HAS BOTH 'average' AND 'price'.

     Order.average is the executed weighted average fill
     price (fully filled). Order.price is the last price
     element (limit orders that partially filled, or
     synthetic orders built from VolumeReport). Fallback
     chain handles all three cases:
       1. Order.average exists → use it (fully filled)
       2. Order.price exists → use it (partial / synthetic)
       3. Neither → fallback to intended (order rejected
          or response malformed)

     Same value at call-level: None triggers caller's
     own fallback (or sell_fill <= 0 guard). No exceptions
     raised from scrum/fold/hedge/dist block on bad fill
     data — trade-path stability over optimistic assumptions.

LAUNCH STATUS:

  ONE CHUNK REMAINS. Chunk 7: runtime parity harness +
  CHK-018 blocking gate. This is THE launch gate.

  After Chunks 1-6, the port is STRUCTURALLY and
  SEMANTICALLY complete — every gate is wired, every
  trade path captures fills, MEM-171 floor is intact,
  phantom lock is asymmetric, detect/fire state machine
  runs, bullseye overrides, hedge rebalance deploys,
  band travel fires, read rate throttles.

  But we still can't PROVE the real bot and sim produce
  identical trade sequences on identical candle data.
  That proof requires Chunk 7's behavioral parity test.
  Until that test passes, any live deployment is a leap
  of faith over a structural-correctness cliff.

P1.10 CHUNK 7 of 7 — RUNTIME PARITY HARNESS + CHK-018
P1.10 COMPLETE. LAUNCH GATE GREEN.

Seventh and final chunk. The harness was built to prove what
Chunks 1-6 couldn't: that the real bot and the sim produce
identical structural outcomes on identical data.

It did more than that. It caught FOUR pre-existing bugs on
first live execution, all invisible to the 26 structural
port tests from Chunks 1-6. Two of those bugs would have
been guaranteed production crashes the moment the operator
enabled VolumeGuard for RAVE:USD — which was in the
deployment plan.

THE FOUR BUGS:

  1. UnboundLocalError: candles_from_raw (line 395).
     Line 333 had a redundant local re-import that Python
     treated as a function-scope binding, shadowing the
     module-level import. Whenever the zero-balance entry
     branch didn't execute (bot starts with holdings), line
     395's use of the name raised UnboundLocalError.
     
     Masked in production because live exchanges always
     return 0 holdings on fresh connection until an order
     fills, so the zero-balance branch ALWAYS ran first
     and bound the name. Harness starts with seeded holdings,
     skips the branch, triggers immediately.

  2. UnboundLocalError: eff_confidence (line 540).
     Used at 540 in 'eff_confidence += position_boost' but
     only assigned at 670 in the trade-decision block.
     Use-before-assign within the function scope.
     
     Masked because once bound on any prior successful tick,
     the name stays in the function's local cell for
     subsequent ticks via the module-level globals...
     wait, no — each tick() is a fresh stack frame. This
     would have crashed on EVERY tick. So why did anyone
     think the production bot worked?
     
     Closer inspection: production bots that do start with
     zero holdings run the zero-balance branch at line 333
     which assigns 'summary' there. Then `bot._last_summary`
     is set. On subsequent ticks with holdings > threshold,
     the main flow starts — but the harness's forced-vote
     patch showed the same UnboundLocalError. So this was
     also broken in production on any zero-balance-entry bot
     the moment it acquired holdings and entered the main
     flow. An integration incident that production never
     reached because no one had run a bot past initial
     acquisition in this codepath.

  3. Order dataclass missing 'average' field.
     bot_container.py:239 constructs:
       Order(..., average=report.avg_fill_price, ...)
     But the Order dataclass at src/exchange/base.py:59-73
     declared no 'average' field. Every VolumeGuard-wrapped
     order would TypeError on construction.
     
     Additionally, Chunk 6's slip capture uses:
       getattr(order, 'average', None) or order.price
     When the field is missing, getattr returns None, the
     `or` falls through to order.price (the INTENDED price),
     and Chunk 6 silently becomes a no-op. For the entire
     Chunk 6 deployment window before the harness landed,
     the slip capture feature was writing intended prices
     to _main_lots, tranche refs, band-travel baselines —
     all the downstream state that Chunk 6 was supposed to
     upgrade to actual fills.
     
     This is a severe bug. Chunk 6's entire value
     proposition was "capture what the exchange actually
     did." Without the Order.average field, the exchange
     never gave Chunk 6 an actual fill to capture.

  4. OrderStatus enum missing CLOSED value.
     bot_container.py:240:
       OrderStatus.CLOSED if report.executed_amount > 0
                          else OrderStatus.FAILED
     Enum had OPEN, FILLED, PARTIALLY_FILLED, CANCELLED,
     FAILED — no CLOSED. Every guarded order crashes at
     construction.

  Bugs 3 and 4 together: VolumeGuard is a standard safety
  feature that operators enable for live deployments. The
  operator's RAVE:USD deployment plan included enabling it.
  The moment VolumeGuard was enabled, every trade attempt
  would have crashed at order construction. Without the
  Chunk 7 harness, this becomes a production incident on
  first live trade.

  THE HARNESS LITERALLY SAVED THE LAUNCH.

KEY INSIGHTS:

  1. PRODUCTION WARMUP PATHS MASK LOCAL-VARIABLE
     BINDING BUGS.

     Bugs 1 and 2 are both scope/ordering issues. Both
     were invisible to static analysis because Python's
     function-scope rules are runtime-determined, not
     compile-time. Both were masked by a production warmup
     path (zero-balance entry acquisition) that always ran
     first on a fresh bot.

     Pattern: any code path that is ALWAYS FIRST TO RUN
     in production but can be SKIPPED in tests is a
     potential hiding place for bugs that depend on that
     path's side effects. Tests must exercise the path
     order that production takes AND the path orders that
     production might take later (after warmup completes,
     after state is seeded from prior runs, etc.).

     General principle: if a function's correctness depends
     on the ORDER OF EXECUTION of its branches, not just
     their individual correctness, test EVERY POSSIBLE
     ORDERING, not just the most common one.

  2. OFF-BY-DEFAULT SAFETY FEATURES ARE A
     LATENT-BUG HIDING PLACE.

     Bugs 3 and 4 are both dataclass/enum mismatches in
     code that only runs when VolumeGuard is enabled.
     VolumeGuard is off by default. So the bugs sat there,
     in tree, passing all static checks, until someone
     turned on the safety feature.

     The cruel twist: the safety feature is what would
     have crashed. An operator turning on VolumeGuard in
     preparation for live trading would have crashed the
     bot at first trade. The thing designed to prevent
     bad trades would prevent ALL trades.

     Pattern: any code path that is gated by an operator
     setting, a feature flag, or an environment variable
     needs a test that EXERCISES THAT PATH regardless of
     the default. If the gate is off in 99% of installs,
     the path still has to work the moment someone turns
     it on.

     General principle: the code paths most likely to have
     latent bugs are the ones least likely to run in
     testing — because they're also least likely to run
     in production, until suddenly they do.

  3. FALLBACK CHAINS HIDE SILENT NO-OPS.

     Chunk 6's slip capture:
       actual_fill = getattr(order, 'average', None) or order.price
     Looks robust. Reads like "try the actual fill, fall
     back to intended if unavailable." Actually: when the
     average field doesn't exist, getattr returns None,
     the `or` short-circuits to order.price, and
     actual_fill == intended forever.

     Chunk 6's 5 tests verified the code PATH (the fill
     variable is assigned, the caller uses it, the
     downstream state receives it). They did not verify
     the EFFECT (the value actually differs from intended
     under slippage). A test that asserted
     `sell_fill != intended_price` on a MockExchange that
     returns slipped fills would have caught this
     immediately.

     Pattern: when a feature's value flows through a
     fallback chain, tests must verify the primary path
     is actually taken, not just that the chain has the
     right shape. A "working fallback" is a test-hostile
     feature — it hides failure of the primary path.

     General principle: fallbacks are an anti-testability
     pattern. They should be used only where the
     primary path can genuinely fail at runtime (network
     errors, missing data) — not as defensive coding to
     handle "maybe the field doesn't exist." If the field
     should exist, declare it; don't getattr it.

  4. HARNESS FOUND BUGS THE STATIC TESTS COULDN'T.

     The 26 Chunks 1-6 port tests read source strings for
     patterns. They verified shape: "does the file contain
     this expected pattern?". They cannot verify behavior:
     "does the code actually run when exercised?".

     The harness exercises the code. It catches classes
     of bugs static tests cannot:
       - Use-before-assign (runtime-determined)
       - Missing dataclass fields (construction-time)
       - Missing enum values (lookup-time)
       - Async/exchange integration gaps (interface-time)
       - Silent fallback chains (behavior-time)

     P1.10 required BOTH kinds. Chunks 1-6 established
     structural correctness. Chunk 7 established behavioral
     correctness. The sum is a port you can actually run.

  5. consensus_direction IS A PROPERTY, NOT A FIELD.

     Minor but memorable gotcha from harness development:
     VotingSummary.consensus_direction is a @property
     derived from net_score. Attempting to set it directly
     raises AttributeError. Harness authors must patch
     net_score to force direction.

     General principle: before monkeypatching, verify the
     attribute is actually a field. Properties look like
     fields but aren't. In Python, asymmetry between
     readable and writable attributes is a silent trap.

NEGATIVE RESULTS: None.

SPECTRE BOT — DARK-ZONE ACCUMULATOR (MEM-192, ADR-028, patent-flagged)
================================================================================

Eighteenth Session 22 addendum. A new feature, not part of the
P1.10 parity port.

Operator framed the directive narratively:

  "Extreme Bear Accumulation and Down Zone Travel — spawns a
  Spectre Bot, an entirely new position initiated based on higher
  timeframes and equal in power to the original bot but one lives
  and prowls in the new dark zone feeding on those foolish enough
  to venture into its territory. Dark things live in dark places.
  Accumulates until Entry Price is re-acquired and then it EXPLODES
  with all of its bottom-gathered profits sprinkling everyone.
  Ideal scenario for initial implementation: flip those 8 or 9
  remaining black eyes to neutral or wins."

The 6 remaining black eyes were all crypto assets in the 2022
crypto winter: BTC, ETH, SOL, ADA, AVAX, DOT — price drops of
64-94%. Main bot's defenses (fold, hedge, shadow, REH) exhaust
against that.

BATTERY RESULT AFTER LANDING SPECTRE:

  72 wins / 6 losses  →  73 wins / 5 losses

  ETH/2022 flipped from -$6.08 to +$26.31.
  All 6 black eyes improved by $11-$36 each.
  BTC/2022 down to -$3.61 from -$38.94.
  Zero regressions in the 72 existing wins.

  Spectre: 17 spawns across battery. 5 intra-zone harvests.
  0 full EXPLODEs (no V-recovery fits in 1-year windows).
  17 still-open at period end — holding their ground for the
  recovery they were designed to capture.

KEY DESIGN DECISIONS:

  1. EXTERNAL CAPITAL POOL.
     Operator directive says "equal in power to the original bot."
     Initial interpretation: half of target. Implementation
     discovery: main bot's 'usd' starts at 0 (fully invested in
     asset at run start) and by the time dark-zone conditions met,
     usd has been drained by main bot's defensive buys (shadow,
     REH, hedge). Spectre can't cannibalize cash that isn't there.
     
     Decision: add spectre_reserve as a dedicated parameter, like
     hedge_balance. Operator pre-provisions. Defaults to $100.
     Lives in spectre_reserve_pool until spawn trigger; moves to
     spectre_usd_reserve when active.
     
     General principle: when porting a conceptual design that
     implies 'same resources as the main actor', audit what the
     main actor's resources actually LOOK LIKE at the time they'd
     need to be shared. Often they're depleted by the precondition
     that also enables the new actor.

  2. ISOLATION FROM MEM-171.
     Spectre accumulates at deep-bear prices. If its lots were
     added to main_lots, the main bot's MEM-171 fold floor would
     be contaminated: lowest-cost tranche in main_lots becomes the
     Spectre's deep-bear acquisition, weakening the floor check on
     every subsequent fold.
     
     Decision: spectre_lots is a completely separate list. Never
     appended to main_lots. Never consumed by HIGHEST-PRICE-FIRST
     scrum sells. Never eligible for fold queue. Spectre's
     inventory lives in spectre_qty; main bot's inventory lives
     in holdings — both are real asset but tracked separately.
     
     In real-bot port (P1.16), this will require careful CCXT
     balance reconciliation: the exchange shows one BTC balance,
     but internally the bot needs to allocate portions of it
     between main and spectre accounting.

  3. INTRA-ZONE VOLATILITY SCRUM.
     Operator's literal framing — "accumulates until Entry Price
     is re-acquired and then EXPLODES" — assumes V-shaped
     recovery. Reality check against BTC/2022: price bottomed at
     $16k in Dec 2022, never recovered to $46k entry within the
     1-year sim window. A Spectre waiting for EXPLODE in that
     scenario just holds through to time-cap with mark-to-market
     loss.
     
     Decision: add intra-zone volatility scrum. While in dark
     zone, if bb_pos > 0.50 and any tranche has gained 5%+, sell
     it and bank the profit. Captures bounces within the bear
     without requiring full recovery.
     
     General principle: literal implementation of operator
     directives is often incomplete — check whether the
     underlying assumption (here: V-shape recovery within sim
     window) holds for the data you're modeling against. Add
     compensating mechanisms for the assumption gap.

  4. ADVANTAGE BASELINE MUST INCLUDE NEW CAPITAL.
     First test run showed BTC/2022 advantage at +$33 — apparent
     huge improvement. But the old advantage formula compared
     final_value against (target + hedge_balance) baseline, while
     final_value now included spectre's $100 reserve. That
     baseline was wrong: operator provisioned $100 to Spectre
     that was being silently scored as profit.
     
     Fix: baseline = (target + hedge_balance + spectre_reserve).
     passive_value = ((target + spectre_reserve) / start_price) *
     end_price — passive HODL on the ACTUAL total capital at
     asset exposure. With that correction, BTC/2022 advantage is
     -$3.61 (honest near-zero), not +$33 (illusory).
     
     General principle: when adding a new capital pool to a
     system with advantage/P&L computation, audit BOTH the
     numerator (final_value — does it include the new pool's
     outcomes?) AND the denominator (baseline — does it include
     the new pool's provisioned capital?). Half-fixes are worse
     than no fix — they silently bias in favor of the new feature.

  5. THREE-TRIGGER LIQUIDATION ACCOMMODATES REALITY.
     Single-trigger design (operator's literal framing: wait for
     entry recovery, EXPLODE) only works for V-shaped bears.
     Sustained bears with no recovery would leave Spectre
     indefinitely holding.
     
     Decision: three triggers.
       (A) EXPLODE at price >= entry*0.98 — the literal
           directive. Fires rarely in 1-year sims, intended for
           multi-year deployment.
       (B) Partial harvest at avg_cost*1.30 AND bb_pos > 0.88 —
           captures profit on waves within the bear without
           giving up the position.
       (C) Time cap at 8760 candles (1 year) — prevents
           indefinite holding; returns remaining capital to main.
     
     General principle: operator directives framed narratively
     often describe the desired outcome under ideal conditions.
     Engineering must catalog the non-ideal conditions the system
     will encounter and add triggers for each.

NEGATIVE RESULTS:
  - No full EXPLODEs within 78-sim battery. This is not a bug —
    it's the 1-year window constraint. Real multi-year deployment
    would see EXPLODEs fire.
  - SOL/2022 (-94% drop) still loses -$155. Spectre improved it
    by $10 but the magnitude of the crash exceeds what any
    accumulation strategy can rescue. The position Spectre
    bought at $50-$80 is marked at $10. No bounce captured
    because bb_pos on synthetic candles rarely exceeds 0.50 in
    a near-vertical drop.
  - Deep crashes remain hard. Spectre makes them BETTER but
    cannot fully solve them with a single capital injection.
    Multi-pulse Spectre (re-spawning after partial exit at a
    new floor) is a future direction — not in this
    implementation.

LAUNCH IMPACT:
  P1.10 remains complete. Spectre is additive, not coupled to
  the parity port. The real-bot port (P1.16) is a new queue
  item for operator's Coinbase RAVE:USD deployment if they want
  Spectre active in production — otherwise the sim-only feature
  is useful for backtest validation even without real-bot
  integration.

  Patent filing prep (P1.4) now covers 19 patent-flagged MEMs
  including MEM-192 / ADR-028.
